overview: Physics Sim is a browser-based MuJoCo rigid-body physics simulator. Scenes are defined as a tree of SceneNode bodies, each with primitive geoms and joints. The simulator compiles scenes to MJCF XML and runs MuJoCo WASM in the browser. Coordinate system: X=right, Y=forward/depth, Z=up. Ground plane at Z=0.
workflow: 1. Call physics_get_schema to understand available geom/joint types and fields.
2. Use physics_build_scene (easy, auto-fills defaults) or physics_update_scene (full control).
3. For an organic or particular shape (a face, an animal, a worn tool) use physics_create_sculpt and physics_sculpt rather than primitives or OpenSCAD. See schema.sculpting.
4. For a crisp dimensioned part (a bracket, a housing, a mount) use physics_create_lattice and physics_lattice_extrude: exact coordinates on a grid. See schema.lattice.

5. Use physics_run_headless to simulate N ticks and verify behaviour programmatically: check final positions, velocities, or trajectory shape against expected values. Do this before relying on visual inspection.
6. Call physics_play to show the simulation to the user once you have confirmed it behaves correctly via headless run.

7. Call physics_set_note_cards to put a card on the scene describing what was built: its title, its dimensions, and the physics it demonstrates. A scene without one is not finished; see that tool's description for the shape of a good card.
8. Use physics_set_environment to adjust gravity, wind, floor friction, and fluid density.
gotchas: HOLLOW SHAPES NOW COLLIDE AS HOLLOW SHAPES, so do not build proxy walls. MuJoCo itself collides a mesh as its CONVEX HULL, which fills in any cavity — a cup, bowl, open-top box, funnel or housing would be solid and a ball dropped in would rest on an invisible lid at the rim. The app now measures each body's SOLIDITY (true volume over hull volume) and breaks anything below ~0.92 into convex pieces automatically, for every kind of mesh body: imported STL, sculpt, lattice, relief, SCAD, boolean. Model the container as a container. physics_get_scene_summary reports `collidesAs` and `solidity` per body, and `cavityFilled` when a hollow body is still colliding as its hull. Override with `collision`: 'hull' forces the old filled-in behaviour, 'decompose' forces the split. A NARROW SLOT CAN STILL BE BRIDGED by one piece while the body looks healthy ("9 convex pieces"): the app now checks every decomposition for cavities a piece fills in, retries once at finer detail when it finds one, and reports any left as `cavitiesFilled` (centre, extent and volume in mm, and the collider covering it) in physics_get_scene_summary. If one remains, raise `collisionResolution` (V-HACD voxels, default 25000, up to 400000) and/or `collisionHulls` (pieces, up to 64) on the body rather than adding hidden proxy boxes. ONE CONSEQUENCE: a decomposed hollow body is weighed by its true volume rather than its hull's — often a third as much — so set `mass` or `collisionMass` if you wanted the heavier figure.

A body that looks TRANSPARENT or see-through is rarely a transparency setting. Check its rgba alpha (below 1 draws translucent); if that is 1, the usual cause is inside-out face winding, because mesh geoms are drawn single-sided: the near surface is culled and you are looking at the inside of the far wall through the gap where it should be. Call physics_get_scene_summary and read `windingInverted` on the geom before you touch colours or materials.

DO NOT add a body with a plane geom as a floor. MuJoCo provides a built-in ground plane at Z=0 automatically. Adding a plane body causes a silent compile error: the scene loads but physics_play returns ok:true while isPlaying stays false. Omit the floor body entirely.

After calling physics_play, immediately call physics_get_state and check that isPlaying is true. If it is still false, the scene failed to compile (likely a bad geom, duplicate name, or plane body conflict). Fix the scene and try again.
Script functions require the 'api.' prefix. Writing getTime() instead of api.getTime() throws ReferenceError and silently breaks the script. All api calls must be api.functionName(...).
To give a body an initial velocity, use a script with a first-tick guard: if (api.getTime() === 0) { api.setVelocity([...], 'bodyName'); }. Using === 0 fires exactly on the first tick.

The script field on a SceneNode is a single string: 'script': '...'. It is NOT an array. Passing scripts:[{code:'...'}] or scripts:['...'] will silently be ignored and the script will never run. Always use the singular 'script' key with a flat string value.

Bodies that should NOT collide with each other (e.g. windmill blades, rotor hub, nacelle) MUST have contype:0 AND conaffinity:0 on ALL their geoms. Without this, sibling bodies that overlap near a shared parent origin generate huge contact-constraint forces that oscillate and prevent scripted torques from accumulating. Even a few millimetres of geom overlap near the hub causes ±1 rad/s oscillation that prevents spin-up.

api.getOrientation() returns the 9-element row-major rotation matrix of the body the script is attached to (xmat). Column 0 = [R[0], R[3], R[6]] is the body's local X-axis in world space. For a rotor with hinge axis=[1,0,0], project wind onto this axis to get the effective wind speed: Vw = windX*R[0] + windY*R[3].

physics_update_scene's sceneGraph parameter is a bare array of SceneNode objects (matching physics_build_scene's bodies convention), NOT { nodes: [...] }. Passing the wrapped object form is tolerated but the array form is canonical.

physics_build_scene and physics_update_scene wait for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for a final MJCF recompile before responding, and report the real result as { ok, error?, nodeCount }. There is no need to poll physics_get_state afterward. The call can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies (each compiles sequentially).

physics_get_state.lastCompileError holds the most recent MJCF/MuJoCo compile error message (or null on success). Check this after loading a scene to see the real underlying failure reason instead of just a generic ok:false.

OpenSCAD designs in this simulator must be scaled to meters (scale([0.001, 0.001, 0.001]) { ... }) at the top-level. Leaving them in default millimeters causes meshes to render 1000x too large, breaking camera zoom bounding boxes and physics stability.

To visually verify layout, spacing, or alignment of a scene, use the physics_get_screenshot tool directly rather than launching a Puppeteer or browser instance. Spawning browser instances is slow, resource-heavy, and redundant when the direct viewport screenshot tool is available.

FOR LETTERING ON A PART, USE physics_apply_pattern WITH pattern: 'text', NOT OpenSCAD text() AND NOT HAND-BUILT LETTERS. It engraves or embosses real lettering in any Google font (fontFamily, fontWeight, heightMm), straight, round an arc, along a wave or any SVG path, on any face of any body — flat, curved or a cylinder's side — and it exports to STL, 3MF, relief carving and machining like the part. Or pass it at build time as `patterns: [{ at, normal, pattern: 'text', options: { text, fontFamily, heightMm }, depthMm }]` on the body. OpenSCAD's text() is unreliable in the browser compiler (it can compile silently to empty geometry), and stroke-built letters are a workaround from before the text pattern existed.

When performing CSG difference operations in OpenSCAD (such as cutting slots, grooves, or recesses), ensure the subtracted geometries extend slightly past the outer boundaries of the main body. Perfectly coplanar faces at the cutting limits can cause degenerate triangles or rendering artifacts (like flickering or jagged ridges) in the WebGL renderer.
To load a user preset, use the 'user:presetName' format (e.g. 'user:mukada') in the physics_load_preset parameter. The bridge handles this automatically by pulling from localStorage.

If a dynamic mesh's visual representation is misaligned or hovering compared to its collision behavior, verify the renderVertices: they should be a direct swap: (x, -z, y) of the Y-up collision vertices without subtracting the centroid (since MuJoCo handles centroid offset internally).

Never bypass the MCP API surface by creating raw browser agents or Puppeteer connections to query state or localStorage, and do not modify source code files simply to add telemetry/debug commands. Use the existing MCP endpoints to query state (e.g. physics_get_state) and apply updates (e.g. physics_update_scene).

Ensure geom size arrays match the required element count for each primitive: 'capsule' requires 2 elements [radius, half_length] (or use fromto), 'cylinder' requires 2 elements [radius, half_height], 'box' requires 3 elements [hx, hy, hz], and 'sphere' requires 1 element [radius]. A 1-element capsule with no fromto does NOT error and does NOT disappear: the MJCF writer falls back to half_length = radius, so the intended rod/spoke/arm silently becomes a tiny stub pill at the geom's pos. Since such geoms usually also default to pos:[0,0,0], several of them (e.g. the five arms of a star) stack into ONE small blob at the body origin. A single unexplained capsule at the centre of a body is almost always this, not a renderer or simulator fault. Inspect the geoms with physics_get_object and look for 1-element capsule sizes.

Visual geoms and bodies (such as capsule rods, hub rings, bearings, and axle pins) mounted near shared joint pivot origins MUST have contype:0 AND conaffinity:0 set on their geoms. Without contype:0/conaffinity:0, overlapping geoms near the pivot origin generate strong contact interpenetration forces that lock the joint and cause high-frequency wobbling in place instead of smooth swinging.
When constructing or updating hinge joints, always explicitly specify the rotation axis (e.g. axis:[0,1,0]). Omitting axis causes MuJoCo to default to [0,0,1], breaking planar hinge motion.

When mutating or generating scene nodes, preserve existing capsule span attributes (fromto or 2-element size), collision flags (contype:0/conaffinity:0), and joint axes so rods and pivots do not disappear or jam after scene updates.

When generating parametric OpenSCAD scripts (such as sine waves, splines, or ribbons), ALWAYS declare design parameters (e.g. wave_length = 50; // [10:5:200], thickness = 2.0; // [0.5:0.5:10]) on separate lines at the VERY TOP of the SCAD code, outside any scale(), module, or function blocks. Include Customizer range annotations // [min:step:max] so the app can automatically parse them into interactive UI sliders.
Copilot response parsing rule: diagnostic 'questions' arrays (containing question/options keys) must NEVER be treated as scene 'nodes'. Scene nodes require valid body/geom/scad structure.

A body with a 'scad' script compiles to exactly ONE mesh geom that IS the entire part. The SCAD source is the single source of truth for that body's shape. When converting a primitive-built body to SCAD, or rewriting its SCAD, you MUST also replace its geoms array with just that one mesh geom. Leftover primitives from the previous version are not ignored: they still render and still collide on top of the mesh, and because they are typically unpositioned (pos:[0,0,0], no fromto) they pile up at the body's centre as stray blobs and discs that look like simulator artefacts. Note that physics_update_object with a 'scad' payload only refills the existing mesh geom; it does NOT prune sibling primitives, so send an explicit geoms array to remove them. A dynamic mesh already collides via its convex hull, so do not keep primitives around 'for collision' unless you want a proxy. In that case position it explicitly and set contype:0/conaffinity:0 on whichever geom must not collide.

Do not use rgba alpha to hide a helper/bounds geom. Alpha below 1 draws a geom translucent, and 0 makes it invisible, but either way it still collides and still has mass: an invisible bounds box is a wall nothing can pass through. If a geom should not be there, delete it.

THE VIEWPORT IS NOT A VALIDATOR. A scene that looks right can still be unusable: open edges, inverted winding, zero-area triangles and shells that merely touch instead of overlapping are all invisible on screen and all break an export. physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt report `watertight` on every reply for exactly this reason — read it. A raw mesh geom you built yourself has no such guard, so check it before you rely on it, and prefer physics_create_lattice or physics_create_sculpt when the thing is going to be made rather than only looked at.

A screenshot is evidence about APPEARANCE and nothing else. It cannot show you that a mesh is closed, that a wall is the thickness you asked for, that two parts are joined rather than overlapping, or that a dimension is what you intended. Use physics_measure for distances, the `watertight` flag for solidity, and the export tools' own warnings for whether a part can actually be made.

A CURVED OR ROUNDED MESH RESTING FLAT ON A BOX OR ANOTHER MESH CAN START MOVING BY ITSELF. MuJoCo 3.8's convex collision gives a mesh-on-box or mesh-on-mesh pair ONE contact point, so a flat-bottomed rounded part (a phone, a tile, a puck) is balanced on a point: measured on a 75 x 150 x 8.5 mm rounded slab lying on a box, it sat still for 2.5 s and then slid and spun at about 6 mm/s and 7 deg/s. The same slab on the floor plane stays put, and as a box primitive on the box it gets four contacts and stays put. A leaning mesh also creeps (0.17 mm/s down a wall). The fix is a box collision proxy on the resting body — a box geom sized to the flat face, with contype:0/conaffinity:0 on the mesh so only the box collides (alpha 0 hides the box) — not solver settings: an elliptic cone stops the leaning creep but makes the flat case worse, and disabling native CCD fixes the flat case but quadruples the creep. physics_run_headless's `final` (settled/rocking) tells you whether a resting pose really is at rest.

MOLDS INVERT. A casting copies the master, but the mold is turned over to pour into: whatever the master stands on in a pour box becomes the casting's pour face, and the master's top ends up at the bottom of the mold. For anything with a right way up (text, a logo, a face, relief art), settle which end of the finished casting is its top before building the master, and when checking a simulated cast, turn it the way it will stand first. Neither physics_make_pour_box nor physics_add_simulation knows which way up the piece is meant to be used.

coordinateSystem.mujocoWorldSpace: X=right (+X right, -X left), Y=forward into screen (+Y away, -Y toward viewer), Z=up (+Z height). Ground plane at Z=0. Gravity default: Z=-9.81.
coordinateSystem.geomPos: pos field on geoms is a local offset from the body origin in MuJoCo Z-up space.
coordinateSystem.bodyPos: pos field on bodies is relative to parent body (or world origin for root bodies).
coordinateSystem.meshVertices: EXCEPTION: mesh geom vertices are in Three.js Y-up world space (X=right, Y=up, Z=toward camera). See mesh section.
coordinateSystem.cameraOrientation: CAMERA Y-AXIS RULE: In MuJoCo world space, -Y is in front of the object toward the viewer, and +Y is behind the object. To frame a front-on view of an object at target [0, 0, z], set position to a NEGATIVE Y coordinate (e.g. position: [0, -2.5, z], target: [0, 0, z]). Passing a positive Y coordinate (e.g. [0, 2.5, z]) places the camera behind the object looking into empty space.
coordinateSystem.defaultCamera: physics_get_screenshot always renders whatever the viewport camera currently shows. Use physics_set_camera(position, target), both MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z], to point the camera at a specific body/face before screenshotting. To frame a front-on view of an object at [x,y,z], place position at a negative Y offset relative to target (e.g. position:[0, y-2.5, z], target:[x, y, z]). For a square-on view of the whole scene, preset 'front', 'side' or 'topDown' gives an orthographic drawing view, and dims:true marks it in mm. The default 'perspective' preset is a diagonal 3/4 pose. physics_get_camera returns the camera's live pose.

tools.list_sessions:
List the browser tabs connected to each app, and say which one commands are going to.

Several tabs of the same app can be open at once. Without this the hub could only shout at all of them and keep whichever answered first, which makes the app look haunted: a body created by one call is missing from the next, a preset saved over a good one comes back empty, a screenshot shows a scene from twenty minutes ago. Each tab now has an id and a label, and every command goes to exactly one of them.

The most recently connected tab is selected by default, so with one tab open there is nothing to do. With several, call this and then use_session.
tools.physics_add_object:
Add ONE body to the scene, leaving everything already in it alone. `body` is a single body descriptor, exactly the shape of one element of physics_build_scene's `bodies` array, and the same defaults are filled in.

Use this instead of reading the scene back and posting it again through physics_update_scene. On a scene holding a sculpt or a boolean that round trip is megabytes each way, and it overwrites anything another client changed in between. physics_delete_object is the other half of the pair.

parent (an existing body's id or name) puts the new body inside that one instead of at the top level. Its pos is then relative to the parent, and with no joints given it is fixed rigidly to the parent and moves with it. Give it a hinge or slide joint to let it turn or slide; a free joint is refused, because MuJoCo allows one only at the top level. The same rule holds for nested children in physics_build_scene: a child with no joints is fixed to its parent.

An id that is already taken is given a numeric suffix rather than refused, and the reply says what the body was actually called. The reply also carries the real MJCF compile result, so a body that failed to build says so rather than reporting ok and leaving you to find out.
tools.physics_build_scene: Build and load a scene from simplified body descriptors. Auto-fills safe defaults. Easier than physics_update_scene. Waits for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for MJCF to settle before responding. The response is { ok, error?, nodeCount }, so check `ok`/`error` directly rather than polling physics_get_state. Can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies. After the scene lands, write its note card with physics_set_note_cards; nothing else does. The default card says "Interactive 3D rigid-body physics scene". Replace it as part of building the scene.
tools.physics_carve_scene:
Machine the scene that is loaded. Needs the machine armed. This is the one that cuts.

A solid is machined from more than one SIDE, and the sides are separate programs with the part re-fixtured in between — so this runs ONE side and says which. `side` picks it; the default is the first. Do not treat a carve as a single button press: tell the user the part has to be turned over and the next side run separately, and that Z must be re-zeroed after it is.

`toolDiaMm` (default 3), `sides`, `stockThicknessMm` and `material` shape the program. It refuses if more than 5% of the part cannot be reached by the chosen tool — that comes out as an unmachined lump and the operator finds out three hours in; use a smaller tool, cut from more sides, or pass `acceptUnreachable: true` if that is understood and wanted.

Over a Tekno Box the device runs the program itself and the carve survives the laptop being shut. Over USB this browser is the streamer and the job lives as long as the tab. Poll physics_machine_status for progress — and note that progress is reported as an elapsed clock against an estimate, not as a line count, because a rapid across the stock and a raster pass are both one line and take wildly different times. Without stockThicknessMm it carves in the bench stock (physics_set_environment) when the part fits in it, and says so; a part taller than the bench stock gets stock sized from the part. A framing lap frames the same job the last carve asked for.
tools.physics_check_collisions: Check for initial axis-aligned bounding box overlaps/interpenetrations between scene bodies at t=0 before running simulation.
tools.physics_clear_paint: Remove brushed paint. With no id, strips every stroke in the scene; with an id, that body; with an id and a geomName, that geom. Base colours set by physics_set_color are left alone.
tools.physics_combine:
Merge other bodies into this one and apply a boolean between them. This is how two things you have already built and positioned become one part.

A boolean is a program over ONE body's shapes, so two bodies can never cut each other however they overlap. This brings them together: each merged body's shapes are rewritten into the target's frame — keeping their exact place in the world — marked with the operation, and the bodies they came from are removed, along with anything parented to them.

op 'union' leaves them as ordinary added shapes, which is a compound body needing no boolean at all. 'difference' cuts them out of the target; 'intersection' keeps only the overlap. Both of those turn the boolean on and the result is compiled like any other, so physics_get_object will report csgVolume and the generated source once it has.

Anything can be merged in: a primitive, a lattice part, a sculpt, an imported STL. Build the shape you want to remove, put it where you want it, and subtract it. The target keeps its own id, joints and name.
tools.physics_create_lattice:
Add a lattice body (a shape built by connecting points on a grid) and return its id. This is the only way to make one: a primitive, an imported STL, an OpenSCAD body and a sculpt cannot be converted into one.

Use this rather than sculpting for anything CRISP and DIMENSIONED: a bracket, a housing, a mount, a part that has to be 40 mm across and meet another part squarely.

It starts as a closed box `sizeMm` across (default 40 mm), centred on the body origin. pos is the body's position in world space (default [0, 0, 0.2]); it is dropped in with a free joint, so it falls when the simulation runs. parent (an existing body's id or name) puts it inside that body instead: pos is then relative to the parent, and it is fixed rigidly to the parent. edit:true also opens the lattice tools in the viewport. Only do that when a person is about to carry on by hand: it takes over the viewport and pauses the simulation.

Returns the id and the cage's counts, bounds and size in millimetres. All lattice tools take and return millimetres in the body's own frame, on a 0.1 mm grid.
tools.physics_create_sculpt:
Add a free-form sculptable body, started from clay, and return its id. To brush a shape that already exists - an imported STL, a mesh loaded from a scene file, a compiled OpenSCAD part - pass its id straight to physics_sculpt instead: any mesh body can be brushed. A primitive (box, sphere, cylinder...) and a boolean body cannot; neither has a mesh a stroke would last on.

base picks the starting shape (default 'sphere'); see schema.sculpting.bases for the nine and what each is for. Start from the closest base: 'head' is a bust on its shoulders, 'humanoid' a standing mannequin facing +X. pos is the body's position in world space (default [0, 0, 0.3]); the body is dropped in with a free joint, so it falls when the simulation runs. parent (an existing body's id or name) puts it inside that body instead: pos is then relative to the parent, and it is fixed rigidly to the parent.

Returns the id, the base, and the mesh's vertex/face counts, bounds and size in metres. sizeMm is the clay's longest side in millimetres (default 100). Make it the size of the thing being made - a 70 mm pumpkin is sizeMm 70 - rather than sculpting big and scaling later. physics_resize_sculpt changes it afterwards. physics_sculpt's default radius is a sixth of the body's longest side; go smaller for detail.
tools.physics_cut:
Cut a shape out of a body: a round hole, a rectangular slot, or a spherical dish. Works on ANY body — a primitive, a lattice part, a sculpt, an imported STL — because a cut is an ordinary negative shape added to that body's boolean program.

ON A SCULPT BODY, USE physics_sculpt_cut INSTEAD: a cut made here turns the sculpt into a boolean, and it can no longer be brushed.

THIS IS THE ONLY WAY TO PUT A SHAPE ON A BODY THAT ALREADY EXISTS. A body's geoms are its boolean program, so two separate bodies can never cut each other; physics_combine merges them first if that is what you want.

You say WHERE the cut goes and HOW DEEP, not where the cutter's middle is and how long it is. `at` is a point in the body's own frame in millimetres and `normal` is the outward direction of the surface there (default [0,0,1], straight down onto the top). A line is cast along that normal through `at` to find the material, and `depthMm` is measured from wherever it meets — so 10 mm means 10 mm into the low arm of a bracket as much as into the top of a block. depthMm 0, or omitted, goes right through. The cutter itself is made a little longer than the hole, because a cut ending flush with a surface leaves coincident faces and a boolean of those is not reliably a solid.

`diameterMm` sizes a hole or a dish; `widthMm` and `lengthMm` size a slot, across the surface it enters. A dish is always blind — a ball has no length to run.

The reply gives the point the cut actually landed on, which is not always the point asked for: the line was cast through it to find the surface. NOTE for a lattice body: `at` is the BODY's frame, while physics_get_lattice reports the cage's; the two differ by however far the mesh was recentred on its centre of mass, which physics_get_object reports as latticeOrigin.

WIDTH AND LENGTH ARE IN THE CUT'S OWN FRAME, not the world's. The cutter is made by turning its +Z onto `normal`, so widthMm runs along the surface's local X and lengthMm along its local Y. Cutting straight down (normal [0,0,1]) that is world X and world Y; cutting into a wall facing +Y it is world X and world Z.

TWO CUTS THAT MEET SHOULD OVERLAP, not touch. Negatives that share an exact face leave coincident surfaces in the boolean, and a boolean of those is not reliably a solid. Give neighbouring slots a tenth of a millimetre of overlap and the union comes out clean.

A body that ends up thin and full of through-cuts — a stencil, a fretted plate — may be worth setting to `collision: 'hull'`, which collides it as one filled hull instead of many thin pieces; see the gotcha about hollow shapes.

THE DRAWN SOLID IS NOT WHERE ITS SHAPES SAY IT IS. A compiled boolean is re-origined on its own centre of mass in X and Y, so a plate drawn symmetric about x = 0 with a bore near one edge DRAWS a few millimetres off centre — 4.5 mm, for a 200 mm plate with a 60 mm bore at x = 60. Sizes and the distances between features are exact either way; only the mapping to world space moves.

physics_measure reads the DRAWN scene, so a point measured there has to be converted before it can be cut at: subtract the body's `pos`, then ADD the `csg.originOffsetMm` that physics_get_object and physics_get_scene_summary report. This is the boolean equivalent of `latticeOrigin`, and a lattice body that has also been cut has both.

A TAPPED HOLE: give a hole `threadPitchMm` and it is cut with an ISO 60° thread of that pitch, right-handed unless `threadLeft` is true. `diameterMm` is then the thread's MAJOR diameter — the bolt's name — so an M6 is diameterMm 6, threadPitchMm 1; M3 is 3 × 0.5, M4 is 4 × 0.7, M5 is 5 × 0.8, M8 is 8 × 1.25, M10 is 10 × 1.5. The hole is cut at nominal size: a printed part that must take a real bolt may want a tenth or two of a millimetre on the diameter. Ignored for a slot or a dish. Compiles in well under a second, like any other cut.

HARDWARE: `shape` can also be 'nut_trap', 'counterbore', 'insert', 'insert_boss' or 'bearing', each cut into the part at `at`/`normal` as one feature, sized from ISO tables by `size`: a bolt size 'M2' to 'M24' ('insert' and 'insert_boss' run M2 to M8), or for 'bearing' one of 623, 624, 625, 626, 688, 608, 6000, 6001. nut_trap: a hex pocket the nut drops into (across flats + fitMm, nut height + fitMm deep, default fitMm 0.2) over an ISO 273 clearance hole right through. counterbore: a socket-head recess (DIN 974-1) over a shank hole; `bore` 'clearance' (default) or 'tapped'. insert: a blind hole for a heat-set insert. insert_boss: a round post stood on the face, bored for an insert; `bore` 'insert' (default), 'tapped' or 'clearance'. bearing: a blind pocket at the outer diameter, as deep as the bearing is wide, over a through hole that leaves a ledge under the outer race. `fitMm` is a diametral clearance on what fits in it. The reply gives `group` and the `pieces` it is made of; physics_get_object lists them with a `hardware` tag. Moving or deleting any piece moves or deletes the whole feature. Bolt sizes are not threads: for a plain tapped hole use shape 'hole' with threadPitchMm. `threadFitMm` adds a diametral clearance to a tapped hole.

O-RING GROOVES: shape 'oring' cuts a groove for a stocked O-ring, size 'ID×cord' in mm (e.g. '20×2'; cords 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 5). Where it seals is read off where it is put, or forced with `seal`: on the side of a cylinder it is a 'piston' seal round that boss (sealing inside the bore it goes into); on the wall of a hole a 'bore' seal (sealing on a shaft through it); anywhere else a 'face' seal under a lid, centred on a round face and in the middle of the wall of a round cavity open into it. shape 'seal_cord' cuts a groove that follows the rim of a rectangular face, for O-ring cord cut to length (size = cord diameter, '1.5' to '5'), in the middle of the wall when a box cavity is open into the face. Leave `size` out and it picks the ring or cord that fits. Depth and width are the cord's static gland. A size that cannot fit, or a spot with no room, is refused with the reason. physics_add_hardware kind 'oring' then lays the ring in the groove, and `sealCheck` (in physics_cut's reply and physics_add_hardware's for the ring, and per groove as `sealChecks` in physics_get_object, which is where to look once the lid or bore is in place) says whether it seals against whatever is placed over or round it, with what to change if not: squeeze 15-30%, groove under 85% full, under 5% stretch, and the mating part covering the whole ring.

LINEAR MOTION SEATS: shape 'rail_seat' (size MGN9/MGN12/MGN15, `lengthMm` the rail's, `turned` true to run across the face; `bore` 'insert' (default), 'tapped' or 'clearance' for the bolt holes) cuts a 1.5 mm channel that locates the rail straight with a hole at every bolt. 'rod_clamp' (size the rod's diameter) is a blind socket two diameters deep. 'lm_housing' (size the rod's diameter) is a pocket for its LM-UU bushing with the rod's way right through.

A SMOOTH POCKET OR DISH: shape 'pocket' cuts a recess from its outline, depth and floor, as a dense mesh, so a shallow 112 mm dish comes out smooth instead of stepped like a scaled sphere. outline 'rect' (a rounded rectangle: widthMm, lengthMm, cornerRadiusMm) or 'ellipse' (widthMm, lengthMm; or diameterMm for a round one); depthMm; floor 'flat' (a flat floor meeting the wall in a fillet of floorRadiusMm, default a quarter of the depth) or 'bowl' (a smooth dish). Placed like any cut, by at/normal; widthMm runs along the surface's local X. The reply's `pocket` echoes what was built. In SCAD, `use <physbox/pocket.scad>` gives the same cutter as a module: pocket(width, length, depth, corner_r=0, floor=\"flat\", floor_r=-1, outline=\"rect\"), rim at z=0 going down, millimetres — subtract it with difference().
tools.physics_add_hardware:
Put a piece of BOUGHT hardware in the scene: a ball bearing, a socket head cap screw, a hex nut or a ground shaft. Bought parts are drawn and simulated but left out of every print, mold and machining export and of the DFM check: they are what goes into the part, not the part.

`kind`: 'bearing' (623, 624, 625, 626, 688, 608, 6000, 6001) | 'screw' (M2 to M24, `lengthMm` under the head from the ISO 4762 lengths, `washer` true for an ISO 7089 washer under the head) | 'nut' (M2 to M24) | 'shaft' (diameter '3' to '12' mm, `lengthMm`) | 'oring' (only seated, `into` a body and `group` an O-ring or rim-seal groove: sized and shaped by the groove; cord is cut to the groove's length).

SEATED IN A HARDWARE CUT is the usual way: give `into` (the body) and `group` (the cut's group from physics_cut's reply, e.g. 'bearing1'). The part becomes a child of that body, sized by the cut, placed in it (a bearing flush in its pocket, a nut on the floor of its trap, a screw bearing on its counterbore's floor), rigid to it, and taken out of the contact solver, because the cut holds it, not contacts. It follows the cut when the cut is moved or resized. A bearing's inner race is a body of its own on a hinge along the bore (reply: `innerRaceId`), so whatever is fixed to it turns. A screw in a counterbore is sized to reach into the next hole along its line in another body, and WELDS that body to the one it sits in (reply: `fastens`); with nothing below it reaches 1.5 diameters past the part. Deleting the screw removes the weld it made. `into` without `group` takes the body's first empty cut that fits. `into` a bearing with kind 'shaft' puts a shaft of its bore through the inner race.

Otherwise the part stands on its own at `at` (world, mm) with a free joint and normal contacts.

Changing a seated part's size changes its cut's size too.

LINEAR MOTION. kind 'mgn_rail' (MGN9, MGN12, MGN15; `lengthMm`), 'linear_rod' (rod Ø6-20 with its LM-UU bushing; `lengthMm`), 'drawer_runner' (full-extension, 250-600 mm; size is the length). Each has a moving piece — the rail's carriage, the rod's bushing, the runner's drawer member — that is a body of its own (`<id>_carriage`) on a limited slide, so it stops at the ends. Seat a rail `into` a body's 'rail_seat' cut `group`, a rod into a 'rod_clamp'. Put a body on the moving piece with `fixTo` (its id): it is welded to the piece and slides with it; for a part already in the scene pass `id` (the part) and `fixTo` and nothing else. A body with an 'lm_housing' cut rides the rod on that housing's line: `into` the body, `group` the housing, any kind; the rod's bushing is moved to the housing and the body welded to it, or the reply says why not (no rod on that line, past its travel). DRAWERS: kind 'drawer_runner' `into` a drawer body that stands in its cabinet puts a pair on the drawer's sides, sized to its depth, out of the side it is flush with, the runners fixed in the smallest body round the drawer (as children of it) and the drawer welded to one runner's slide, the other runner following it. The DFM check measures each runner's side space against 12.7 mm.

WHAT TO BUY: physics_get_scene_summary's `hardwareList` counts every bought part (`rows`) and packs bar stock onto the bar lengths it is sold in (`bars`).

ALUMINIUM EXTRUSION: kind 'extrusion' (size '2020', '2040', '3030', '4040', or '2020V' for V-slot; `lengthMm` any length, cut to suit) is a T-slot profile along its own +Z, the real section drawn and its envelope colliding, weighing the maker's kg/m. 'tnut' (size 'M4/6', 'M5/6', 'M5/8', 'M6/8': thread/slot) stands on its own. 'corner_bracket', 'joint_plate' and 'end_tap' JOIN two profiles: give `between: [aId, bId]` (either order). The end of one must stand square on a side face of the other; the piece is fixed to the profile whose side is met and carries a weld to the other (reply: `weldedTo`), so a frame holds together, and deleting the piece removes its weld. A bracket goes in the inside corner (toward the middle of the met profile), a plate across the outside face the two share (`size` 'L20'/'T20'/... to choose; left out, an L near an end and a T across a middle), an end-tap screw through the met profile into the other's tapped end. Sizes follow the profiles. Two profiles that do not meet are refused with the reason. 'vslot_carriage' with `into` a '2020V' profile puts a three-wheel plate on it on a slide joint along the profile, limited to stop clear of both ends. Slots are mate features, so a T-nut or screw dragged to a profile snaps onto a slot's line.

SPRINGS AND MOTORS: kind 'spring' (Ø6×20 to Ø20×60, at its real rate) — its top is a moving piece (`<id>_carriage`) on a slide with that stiffness, stopping at solid height; `fixTo` a body and it is sprung. kind 'stepper' (NEMA17 40, NEMA17 48, NEMA23 56) — face at its origin, shaft up +Z, the shaft (`<id>_shaft`) on a hinge driven by a velocity actuator (`<id>_spin_actuator`) limited to the motor's holding torque, so it stalls under a load past it. Set its speed as you would any actuator's ctrl.
tools.physics_get_edges:
List the edges of a body that can be rounded or bevelled, with an id for each. Call this before physics_round_edges when you want particular edges rather than a group.

Edges are found on the body AS MODELLED — holes cut, booleans done, but before any rounding — so ids stay the same while its roundings change. Each is a straight `line` (fromMm/toMm) or a round `circle` rim (centreMm, diameterMm, axis): the edge of a box, the rim of a hole or a boss. Everything is in the body's own frame in millimetres. `groups` says which of top / bottom / vertical it belongs to (by the world's up, whatever way the body is turned), or 'inside' for an inside corner, where rounding ADDS material (`convex` false). `maxRoundMm` / `maxBevelMm` is the largest size that fits that edge on its own: half the narrower face beside it, or half the gap to the next edge on that face. `roundedBy` is the index of the rounding that already has it.

`unroundable` counts edges that are neither straight nor a full circle (a sculpted crease, a helix) — they are left alone. Sculpt bodies are refused with the reason. OpenSCAD and imported parts work; if an OpenSCAD part's source is edited so that a rounded edge is no longer there, that edge's rounding is dropped (physics_get_object shows edgeRoundsLost) rather than cut where the edge used to be.
tools.physics_round_edges:
Round (fillet) or bevel (chamfer) edges of any part except a sculpt — a primitive, a boolean with holes cut in it, a lattice part, an OpenSCAD or imported part. The finishing step that makes a block look made rather than modelled.

`edges` is 'all' (default: every OUTSIDE edge), 'top', 'bottom', 'vertical' (outside edges too), 'inside' (the inside corners, where rounding adds material — a fillet at the foot of a rib makes it stronger), or a list of ids from physics_get_edges. `sizeMm` is the fillet's radius, or for a bevel how far back along each face the cut starts. `mode` 'round' (default) or 'bevel'. A size bigger than fits is refused, with the largest that does. `remove: true` takes the rounding off those edges instead (no size needed).

Each call adds one rounding to the body (listed in the reply's `roundings`); an edge belongs to one rounding at a time, so rounding an edge again at a new size moves it to the new one. The rounding is part of the body's boolean program, so the drawn mesh, the colliders, the mass and every export (STL, CNC, casting) get the rounded shape. A rounded part with no hole collides as its own hull, so a filleted block really does roll off its corners. Where three rounded edges of the same size meet square (a box corner) the corner comes out as a ball's eighth. Where an outside edge runs into an inside corner that is also rounded (the top of a gusset meeting the fillet at its foot) the outside rounding stops at the top of that fillet, leaving its last few millimetres sharp: separate roundings cannot blend into each other there.

FOR PRINTING, BEVEL THE BOTTOM EDGES rather than rounding them: edges 'bottom', mode 'bevel', 0.5 mm — a rounded bottom edge is an overhang.

Resizing a box through its size moves its roundings with it. The reply includes the new volumeMm3.
tools.physics_repair_mesh:
Repair non-manifold, open, degenerate, or inconsistently wound triangle meshes in the scene.

Welds vertices within weld_tolerance_mm (default 0.01 mm), removes zero-area degenerate triangles and duplicate/opposite-wound triangle pairs, resolves non-manifold edges (3+ incident triangles), fills open boundary edge loops, and fixes inverted shell winding so meshes are watertight and ready for 3D CSG booleans, slicing, or simulation.

id is the body id or name to repair; omit to repair all mesh bodies in the scene. geom_name targets a specific mesh geom on the body. weld_tolerance_mm sets the vertex welding distance threshold in mm (default 0.01). fill_holes (default true) caps open boundary loops with triangulated patches. fix_winding (default true) orients connected shells consistently with positive enclosed volume. remove_duplicates (default true) strips duplicate and zero-volume folded face pairs. remove_degenerates (default true) strips zero-area and collinear sliver triangles.
tools.physics_delete_object: Remove a body from the scene by id, along with everything parented to it. Returns what was deleted and how many children went with it. DESTRUCTIVE and not undoable. Confirm with the user first unless they asked for it.
tools.physics_set_constraint:
Weld one body to another, attach it with a pin, or say what it takes to break the weld off.

`weldTo`/`connectTo` take a body id, null to clear. A weld holds two bodies rigidly wherever they happen to be; a connect pins one point and lets the body swivel about it.

`breakForceN` and `breakTorqueNm` are what the weld survives, in newtons and newton-metres. MuJoCo reports the force it spends holding every weld, so these are real units rather than a made-up scale: a 1 kg body hanging off a weld pulls about 10 N, a few hundred is a sturdy joint, a few tens is decorative. Either limit alone is enough; a weld given only a force limit ignores torque. Pass null to make the weld unbreakable again.

`breakHoldSteps` (default 3) is how many steps in a row the overload must last. A hard contact makes the solver spike for a single step, and without the hold that spike snaps welds that were never really loaded.

BREAKING IS TRANSIENT. It is a simulation event, not an edit: the scene graph still says the part is welded on, so physics_get_scene, exports and share links are unchanged, and physics_reset puts the object back together. Use physics_get_breaks to see what has come apart.
tools.physics_set_impact:
What a body does when it is hit hard: come apart, take a dent, or neither.

Thresholds are in newton-seconds — IMPULSE, i.e. momentum — not force. Contact force in a hard solver is a spike whose height depends on the timestep as much as on the collision, so a force threshold changes meaning when the timestep does. Momentum does not: 0.2 kg arriving at 5 m/s and stopping dead is 1 N*s whatever the solver was doing.

SHATTERING. `shatterImpulseNs` is the blow that breaks the body up; null clears it. The pieces are Voronoi cells of the body's own outline, so they tile it exactly — they weigh what it weighed and start where it was, each carrying the velocity of the part of the body it used to be. `shatterPieces` is 2..24 (default 8), `shatterPattern` is 'radial' (small pieces crowded around the impact, the default) or 'uniform', `shatterSpread` adds outward speed in m/s, and `shatterSeed` fixes which pieces so a scene breaks the same way twice. `shatterDepth` (0 by default, 2 at most) lets the PIECES break again when they land: each shard inherits a threshold scaled to its own share of the body, because a chip held to the whole body's threshold can hardly ever be hit hard enough and reads as armour plating. Pieces of pieces come apart into at most four, and those chips do not collide with EACH OTHER (they still land on and hit everything else), which is what keeps a cascade running in real time. The world holds at most 60 shards at once: a break that would go over cuts fewer pieces, or does not happen. The body must be able to move: something bolted to the scenery cannot be hit hard enough to matter.

DENTING. `dentYieldNs` is the blow that leaves a permanent crater; null clears it. `dentDepthPerNs` is metres of depth per newton-second over the yield, `dentRadius` the crater's radius in metres, `dentMaxDepth` a hard cap. A dent is a displacement of vertices, so a PRIMITIVE has nothing to push in — a box is six numbers the solver evaluates, not eight corners. Setting a yield on one CONVERTS it to the mesh it already looked like, and the reply says so with `convertedToMesh`. Name the surface with `geomName` if the body has several. A plane cannot be dented at all; it is infinite in the solver. A plate given a yield is unmarked by anything under it and cratered by anything over, which is the point: the same plate, two blows, two outcomes.

`pierceImpulseNs` is a second, higher limit past which the surface is HOLED rather than dented — the material under the striker is removed. Keep it well clear of the yield, or there is no range in which the thing behaves like a sheet. The crater's width and shape come from the STRIKER (a flat-ended slug leaves a flat-bottomed pit its own width, a ball a spherical cap) and grow wider as well as deeper with the blow, so the depth rate should be set so that typical impulses land well under dentMaxDepth — a rate that reaches the cap just past the yield makes every blow leave an identical mark and mass stop mattering.

`deformCollision` makes the damage REAL to the solver instead of only visible: things fall through the holes, and an edge worn away stops holding what it used to. It is off by default because it is genuinely expensive — damage reaches MuJoCo by rebuilding the model, and the surface must also be broken into convex pieces each time, since MuJoCo collides a mesh as its convex hull and a hull fills every crater and every hole straight back in. Expect a hitch per blow. Without it:

DENTS AND HOLES ARE COSMETIC. The contact solver keeps using the undented shape, because feeding a deformed mesh back to it means rebuilding the model and that cannot happen at the rate blows arrive.

All of it is TRANSIENT, like a broken weld: the scene graph still holds the whole body, so physics_get_scene, exports and share links are unchanged, and physics_reset makes it whole and unmarked again. physics_get_breaks reports what has actually come apart or been dented.
tools.physics_set_crumple:
A crumple zone: a joint that is rigid until it is overloaded, and then folds and STAYS folded.

Set on a JOINT, because that is what folds — name it with `jointName`, or the body's first hinge or slider is used. A free or ball joint has no single axis to fold about and is refused.

`crumpleTorqueNm` is the torque past which it gives, in newton-metres; null clears it. `crumpleRangeDeg` is how far it may fold afterwards, in degrees, as [min, max]. `crumpleDampingAfter` is the damping written into the joint at the moment it gives — high, normally, so it settles into its new shape rather than swinging into it; without it a released joint reads as a hinge coming undone rather than as metal taking a set.

It costs almost nothing because it is not a new mechanism: the joint is held still by an ordinary weld equality, and giving way is the same release that shears a handle off a mug.

ONE THING TO WATCH: a joint only folds if something is still loading it after it gives. A post standing straight up gives gravity no lever, so once its base yields it simply goes on standing there. A cantilever — an arm held out sideways, already carrying its own weight — folds the moment its root lets go.

TRANSIENT, like every other kind of damage here: the scene graph is untouched and physics_reset straightens it. physics_get_breaks reports it as a key of the form 'crumple:<jointName>'.
tools.physics_get_breaks:
What has sheared off during this run. Returns `broken` (stable keys of the form 'weld:<nodeId>-><targetId>') and `last`, the most recent break with the time and the load it was carrying when it went; `shattered`, the bodies currently in pieces and how many pieces each is in, with `lastShatter`; and `dented`, each marked surface with how many blows it has taken and the deepest in millimetres.

Breakage never reaches the scene graph, so this is the only way to observe it. An empty list means nothing has broken, not that nothing can.
tools.physics_restore_break: Put a broken weld back. With `key`, restores that one joint where the body is now, without disturbing the rest of the run. With no key, resets the whole simulation, which restores everything.
tools.physics_delete_preset: Delete a custom user physics preset by name.
tools.physics_export_cast:
Produce a sand casting pattern for the whole scene and report what the pour needs: part volume, cast weight in the chosen metal, the pattern grown by that metal's shrink, the parting height, the gating sizes, and the share of the part that will not draw from the sand.

metal is one of aluminium, brass, bronze, silver. partingFromBaseMm is a height in millimetres from the base of the part, or 'auto' to let it choose. On a part that is symmetric about its own mid-height, parting at the base makes the entire lower half re-entrant, so 'auto' is worth taking.

Pass out_dir to have the pattern STL written there. Without it you get the numbers and the file sizes only: the mesh itself is never returned into the conversation.
tools.physics_make_pour_box:
Make a printed pour box (mother mold) for casting a silicone mold of a master, the same as the Mold dialog's Silicone pour box: a base plate the master stands on with a groove round it, a sleeve that drops into the groove and holds the silicone, and optionally a wick or pour pin from the master's highest point to 1 mm above the fill line. The master is taken as it stands (poured from above, standing on its lowest point). A pour-box mold is used the other way up from how it was made: the face the master stands on becomes the silicone's open pour face, and the master's top (where the pin is) is at the bottom of the mold while the casting is poured. So for a part with a right way up (text, a logo, a face, relief art), settle which end of the finished casting is its top before building the master, and ask the user if it isn't clear. Art meant to read upright with the pour face as the casting's top goes on the master upside down.

body_id is the master (comma-separated for several bodies; defaults to the selection, else every body). cover_mm (8) is the silicone round the sides and over the top; wall_mm (2.4) the sleeve wall; clearance_mm (0.2) the gap each side of the sleeve in its groove; base_mm (6) and groove_mm (3) the plate and the groove's depth; freeboard_mm (2) the sleeve above the fill line. shape is 'fit' (default: the master's outline grown by the cover, least silicone), 'round' or 'box'. pin=true adds the pin, pin_dia_mm (2.5). silicone is 'platinum' (1.08 g/cm3, 1:1) or 'tin' (1.15 g/cm3, 10:1).

Returns fillHeightMm (above the base, where the master stands), fillZMm, pourDepthMm (the fill as physics_add_simulation kind mold_cast measures it, from the groove floor: pass it as fill_mm to simulate the silicone), sleeveHeightMm, the sleeve and base footprints, siliconeMm3, siliconeG and partAG/partBG to weigh out. apply=true adds the base and sleeve to the scene as static bodies and the pin as a rigid child of the master (one undo step, a note card section); then physics_add_simulation kind mold_cast with body_id '<master>,<base>,<sleeve>' casts the silicone. Pass out_dir to have pour-base.stl and pour-sleeve.stl written there.
tools.physics_set_cast_prep:
Prepare every part in the scene for casting, in the model itself, the same as the Cast dialog's Prepare for Casting switch. Outside edges are chamfered and inside corners filleted (fillet 1.5x the chamfer); for method 'sand' every wall is also given draft away from the parting plane, and the parting face's edges stay sharp. Draft is baked into the parts as meshes, with the originals kept so that off=true restores them; while draft is on, edits to any body are refused with an error naming this tool. Edges go on as ordinary roundings, which physics_get_edges and physics_round_edges see.

method is 'sand' (default) or 'lost-pla' (edges only: a burnt-out pattern needs no draft). draft_deg defaults to 2, draft_mode is 'add' (walls grow toward the parting line, nothing undersize; default) or 'remove'. edges defaults to true; edge_size_mm is the outside chamfer, omitted to size it from each part. parting_from_base_mm as for physics_export_cast. Calling it again re-applies from the originals, so settings never stack. off=true switches it off (bodies changed since prep are left as they are and named); bake=true keeps the prepared shapes and forgets the originals.

Returns how many parts were treated, the largest chamfer and fillet used, edges too short to break, and parts skipped with the reason.
tools.physics_set_reference_image:
Pin a picture in the viewport to model from: a photo of the thing being copied, a drawing, a sketch. It stands in the plane of a drawing view and shows in the viewport and in physics_get_screenshot, so you can line the model up against it and compare the two in one frame. It is only drawn: it takes no part in the physics, any export, the DFM checks or selection. It is saved, shared and undone with the scene.

To add one, pass `path`, an image file on this machine (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF or BMP), read by the server like physics_import_stl's path. It is stored cut down to 1600 px on its long side. To change one, pass the `imageId` an earlier call returned (as `id`), with only the fields to change. `remove: true` with an `imageId` takes that one off; `clear: true` takes them all off.

plane is 'front' (the XZ plane, facing -Y: what physics_set_camera's 'front' preset looks at; the default), 'side' (YZ, facing +X: the 'side' preset) or 'top' (XY, facing up: 'topDown'). The picture reads the right way round from that view. center is the middle of the picture, [x, y, z] in world metres. width is its width in metres; give height instead to size it by its height, and the other follows from the picture's own proportions. With neither, a new picture comes in as wide as the scene's contents and centred on them, standing on the floor (lying on it for 'top').

TO SCALE A PHOTO TO A MODEL, measure in pixels: if a part D mm across spans p pixels of an image W pixels wide, the whole picture is width = W / p x D mm, and its center sits where that part's middle is, offset by the part's distance from the image's middle at the same scale. opacity is 0..1 (default 0.5). overlay (default true) draws the picture over the model so it can be traced; false lets the model hide it. hidden: true keeps it without drawing it.

Returns the picture's id, plane, center, widthMm, heightMm, opacity and overlay, and `referenceImages`: every picture in the scene. physics_get_scene_summary lists them too.
tools.physics_split_for_print:
Cut a body into sections that each fit the 3D printer's bed, the same as the Split for Print dialog (bottom bar, FDM). Each section is turned to whichever way up needs the least support, and the cut faces get joinery: 'dowel' (default) bores matching blind holes in both faces for bought dowels; 'peg' prints a chamfered peg on one face and a hole in the other, the peg going on whichever side's print pose minds it least; 'none' leaves plain faces to glue. Pins are placed as deep in each shared face as they fit, two per face when it is wide enough (so the joint cannot turn), none when the face is narrower than the pin plus min_wall_mm each side (a warning names it).

body_id defaults to the selection. with_ids lists more bodies to split together with it as one part (a box and its lid, say), in body_id's frame; on apply they are replaced by the sections too. Bodies rigidly attached under any of them (children with no joint) are included automatically. bed_mm is [width, depth, height] and defaults to the bed set in the bottom bar (256 cube unless changed). margin_mm (5) is kept clear round the bed edge. diameter_mm (6), length_mm (20, the whole dowel; a peg stands half of it proud), clearance_mm (0.2, on the diameter) and min_wall_mm (2) shape the joinery. The overhang limit comes from the loaded filament.

Without apply it only reports: each section's printed size, support area, pose (up vector and spin), volume (mm3) and hole/peg count; the cuts (normal and offset, body frame); the joints between sections; and exact Manifold checks (overlap between printed sections, mm3; how far the sections differ from the original; pins without a partner). test_assembly=true also puts the sections back together in MuJoCo at print fidelity, one cut at a time: dowels dropped into their holes, then each side dropped onto the other under gravity, then pushed and twisted. Each stage reports gapMm (how far short of its seat it came to rest; about a pin length means a pin missed its hole), playMm and twistDeg ('unbounded' for a plain cut, which glue holds), rotates (a single pin), and notes. apply=true replaces the body with its sections: the first keeps the body's id, the others are new siblings named <name>_part2, _part3..., all in place, coloured apart, carrying printPose (which the 3MF export uses to lay them out on the bed) and exact pin/socket colliders. One undo step.
tools.physics_timber_breakdown:
Break a solid, cabinet or box, or framed furniture (table, chair, flower stand), into wooden parts you can cut on a saw: a cut list with joinery, hardware and a glue-up guide. Optional CNC setups for the pockets.

`mode`: 'auto' (default; frame when it finds legs and rails, planks otherwise) | 'planks' | 'frame'. Targets `body_id` plus `with_ids`, or the selection, or the whole scene.

- PLANKS (box / shell): `hollow_interior` (true: a 6-wall shell of `wall_thickness_mm`, 18; false: solid layers of `board_thickness_mm`, 18). Walls wider than `max_board_width_mm` (180) or longer than `max_board_length_mm` (1200) split along the grain. `joint_type`: 'glue' (flush, no dowels) | 'butt' (with alignment dowels, `dowel_dia_mm` 8, `dowel_length_mm` 30; 0 for none) | 'rabbet' | 'miter' | 'finger' (`finger_width_mm` 24). Returns every plank's size and grain, a lay-flat sheet and a BOM.
- FRAME (legs, rails, top): `joint_mode`: 'mortise_tenon' (default) | 'dowel' | 'dado' | 'glue' (butt joints glued flush, no joinery, no CNC). `tenon_length_mm`, `shoulder_mm`, `tenon_corner_fit` ('dogbone' | 'round_tenon' | 'chisel_square'), `tenon_cut_method` ('bandsaw' | 'cnc'), `edge_profile` ('roundover' | 'chamfer' | 'square') with `edge_radius_mm`, `tabletop_clips` (Z-clip slots in the aprons, M&T and dado only). Wide tops split at `max_board_width_mm`. Returns parts with cut sizes and F1/F2 reference faces, joints, stock bars (`stock_length_mm`, 1800), hardware, a build guide, and CNC setups for the mortises sized to `cnc_bed_mm` [X, Y, Z] (default: the CNC bed in Machine Setup). Pass `include_gcode: true` to get each setup's G-code.

`clearance_mm` is the fit allowance for both. `apply: true` splits the body into one scene body per part (`placement`: 'replace' | 'beside').
tools.physics_export_machining:
Produce a three-axis CNC program for the whole scene and report what the job needs: the stock it wants, the part size and volume, how much of the part no setup can reach, how many holding tabs were placed, the cut distance and the estimated time, plus one G-code program per setup.

sides is 1 or 2. The stock is the bench board (set it with physics_set_environment), as in the dialog: refused, with the size the part needs, when it cannot hold the part; used as it is, the part centred, when it is about the size the part wants; and when it is much bigger, or a side setup needs the block flush with the part, the job is planned on the smaller block and summary.boardPrep says what to cut the board down to first. Per-call stock sizes are refused. toolDiaMm sets both the roughing and the finishing cutter. finishingToolType is the finishing cutter's shape: flat (the default), ball_nose or v_bit. Flat leaves walls square and flats flat, which suits a part made of faces and pockets; a ball nose is what makes a curved surface smooth — a dome, a dish, a sculpted face — where a flat end mill leaves a staircase, at the cost of a radius in every inside corner. Roughing is always a flat end mill. material drives the feeds and speeds: aluminium, hardwood, softwood, plywood, acrylic, foam. The part is cut at its modelled size, millimetre for millimetre, as in the dialog; scale_percent is refused. To cut it bigger or smaller, resize it in the scene. Over 1 m any way is refused with the scale that fits.

SETUPS FROM ANY FACE: setups 'auto' plans as many setups as the part needs instead of sides: it looks at the part from all six faces of the block with the finishing cutter (reaching tool_stickout_mm, or 8 diameters), gives each bit of material to the face it is shallowest under, and keeps the fewest setups that reach the part (it may also lay the part another way up: summary.upChosen). Use it for anything a top-down cut leaves solid: a slot that leans back, the hole in an upright letter, a hook. setups may also be a list of faces, '+z,+x,-x', named as the block stands for setup 1 (+z top, -y front, -x left end). clearance_mm is the room under the spindle; a setup that would stand the block taller than it is left out. The summary then has plan (one line), setups (per setup: face, faceUp, standingHeightMm, depthMm, lengthOverDia, estimatedTimeSeconds, clearedMm3, skinMm left for the turn's error, locate, datum, instructions), remaining (what no face reaches and where; a fillet in corners sharper than the cutter is normal), redesignHint, and dropped faces with the reason. Files are machining-setup-<n>-<face>.nc. Before planning extra setups, prefer a redesign the hint names (make the leaning face vertical): one setup is always cheaper. Only setup 1 can be run over MCP; every later setup is turned and zeroed by the operator at the machine, and the machine refuses it otherwise.

Pass out_dir to have the .nc files written there. Without it you get the numbers and the file sizes only.

It always surfaces the whole part before it profiles it. For something flat that only needs its outline cut — a stencil, a gasket — that is most of the quoted time and none of the useful work.
tools.physics_export_relief:
Plan a relief carve of the scene — the model carved into the top of a board, as the Relief Carve dialog does it — and report how the job splits: the roughing cutter, strategy, layer count and its share of the time, the finishing cutter and pass count, the total estimate, and the 1-based line of the tool change.

By default it uses exactly the settings the Relief Carve dialog last planned with this session — the stock, fit, depth, cutters and any feed typed over — so it reproduces the program the operator would send; optionsFrom says which. If the dialog has not been opened, it starts from the scene's own carve settings and the bench's stock and material.

HEIGHT AND SIZE: by default (vertical_scale_mode 'auto') a model that fits the stock is cut AS MODELLED — 1:1 in X, Y and Z, centred, as deep as the lowest point a cutter coming straight down can see — so a tray, sign or plate with a pattern already on its face needs no depth or scale set at all; carveDepthMm is ignored and summary.heightMode says 'model'. A model bigger than the stock (footprint, or deeper than the stock less 1 mm) falls back to 'fill' (its height stretched onto carveDepthMm, plan fitted to the stock) and a warning says so. Force one with vertical_scale_mode 'model', 'fill' or 'proportional' (with vertical_exaggeration); fit_mode 'fit' (to the stock) or 'actual' (its modelled size, cropped at the stock's edge) sets the plan scale for fill/proportional; scale_percent is refused: resize the model in the scene instead; background_mode 'auto' (leave the stock round a true-size model, carve it otherwise), 'carve' or 'skip'. summary.undercut reports material hidden under an overhang (a leaning slot, a lip) that a 3-axis cut leaves solid: areaMm2, volumeMm3, maxMm, boundsMm. A true-size cut also says it in warnings. Set the bench stock to the real board first (stock_width_mm etc.).

Anything passed is laid on top: roughingToolDiaMm, finishingToolDiaMm, finishingToolType (flat, ball_nose or v_bit), carveDepthMm, material, roughingStrategy (adaptive or raster), roughingEnabled, stockWidthMm, stockDepthMm, stockThicknessMm. Changing a cutter, the material or the depth works the feeds and speeds out again for it. A probed bed is not applied.

Pass out_dir to have relief-carve.nc written there. Without it you get the numbers and the file size only.

An undercut as modelled is not something relief can cut: relief is a single face. Machine it as a part instead: physics_export_machining with setups 'auto' and the same board and cutters stands the block on the faces that reach under the overhang. A feature that runs off the model's edge below the top face (a groove open at both ends) is cut out past the board edge by half a millimetre plus the cutter's radius, and a warning names the edges: keep clamps clear of them.
tools.physics_add_simulation:
Cut a machining, carving, slicing, or mold job back out and add what is left to the scene as a body, to look at, measure and set against the model before any material is spent. The same as the Add Simulation button in the dialogs.

kind picks the job: relief (the program physics_export_relief would hand over, with the same options — vertical_scale_mode, fit_mode and background_mode too and the Relief Carve dialog's last plan by default), machining (physics_export_machining's, with the same stock, both setups, side B turned over as the operator turns it, so holes, tabs and any step at the seam show), laser or contour (the panels or the stacked layers, extruded at material_thickness_mm, which for contour defaults to the bench stock's thickness; with machine='router' every inside corner keeps the bit's radius and a slot narrower than bit_dia_mm is never cut), mold (adds the generated 3D mold to the scene), or mold_cast (simulates what would be cast from a mold — either an existing mold body via body_id or a newly generated mold for the scene — and adds the cast body to the scene; mold_type is 'auto' when not given (a one-part open mold when that keeps the part as well as two halves would, otherwise a two-part clamshell), or 'clamshell' or 'open' to insist; either way the mold opens along whichever of the part's axes fills in the least of it, so an upright bust splits front to back, and the reply names the type and direction it used (moldType, pullDirection, setupNote); trim_channels trims sprue/vent runner stubs).

placement 'beside' (the default) stands the part at the size it comes off the machine beside the model, past any earlier simulation; 'overlay' undoes the fit (scale, and a relief's vertical exaggeration) and lays it over the model, where an over-cut or a missed area is plain.

Returns the body's id and name and the volumes: for relief, what the program removes and how many rapid moves cut material (anything but 0 is a fault in the program); for machining, the part's volume over its footprint against the model's (partVsModel, tabs included); for contour, the stack against the model stretched the same way (stackVsModel); for mold or mold_cast, the mold/cast dimensions, cavity depth, and volume.

The body is static and collides with nothing, gets a section on the scene's note card, and is left out of every later export, so it never changes the next plan. Delete it like any body. A big relief takes a few seconds.

With setups 'auto' (or a list of faces) a machining simulation cuts every setup in its own frame and keeps what all of them leave, so a slot cut from the block's ends shows as cut. One setup, or the top and the flip, are simulated as before. With body_id, pour_direction ('+z', '-z', '+x', '-x', '+y', '-y'; default the best side) and fill_mm (default: to the rim) set the side poured from and how deep; for a silicone pour box from physics_make_pour_box, pass its pourDepthMm as fill_mm. A mold_cast body is set beside the model, not stood the way the finished piece will be used, so its orientation says nothing about which way up the casting is meant to be. Keep track of that yourself, and before judging how text or art reads, turn the body (physics_update_object quat) the way it will actually stand.

For kind mold, dissolvable_liner=true prints the mold as a PLA shell with a dissolvable PVA liner, for a two-filament printer: every undercut is kept, the shell lifts straight off along the pull, and the PVA left on the casting dissolves in warm water. liner_skin_mm (1.2) is the PVA between the casting and the PLA. cast_material is 'epoxy' (the default), 'polyurethane', 'silicone' or 'wax'; the water-based 'plaster', 'concrete' and 'jesmonite' are refused, because they dissolve PVA while they cure. The reply adds liner: pvaGrams, plaGrams, pvaVolumeMm3, castVolumeMl, thickestPvaMm, dissolveHours (a rough guide, at about 1 mm an hour) and the steps to use it; files names the two-material 3MF (PLA shell on filament 1, PVA liner on filament 2, set for Bambu Studio/OrcaSlicer and PrusaSlicer), written to out_dir when one is given.
tools.physics_get_camera: Return the 3D viewport camera's current position and look-at target, both in MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z] (same convention as every other pos field). Reflects the LIVE view, including manual orbiting/panning a human has done in the browser since the last physics_set_camera call or preset change. Call this before a screenshot if you're not sure what's currently framed, or after asking the user to orbit to a specific view themselves. Returns position and target in MuJoCo world space, plus which preset is active. Also returns dims (whether the Dims overlay is on) and dimensions: what it is drawing right now, one entry per figure ({body, kind:'linear'|'diameter'|'radius'|'angle'|'location', direction:'width'|'height', row:'chain'|'overall', count, from, sharedWith, label, valueMm or valueDeg}). Sizes are true sizes along the body's own axes, even when it is turned or tilted; With the viewport's Section button on, the figures are of the cut face of a plane square to the view (depths, wall thicknesses, a round floor's radius), not of the outside; 'radius' is a rounded corner or fillet seen square on (count: how many equal ones); a chain link labelled like '3× 42' stands for count equal steps, valueMm one step; 'angle' is its long axis against the sheet's horizontal or vertical, or a slanted edge's angle from the nearer of them (a draft, a dovetail flank, a gusset; count: how many equal ones), a chamfer labelled like '5 × 45°'; 'location' is its origin from its parent body's origin (`from`, or 'origin'). A figure two bodies share at the same place (walls whose faces line up) is listed once, the other bodies named in sharedWith — empty in perspective, with Dims off, or once the camera is orbited off the view's axis.
tools.physics_get_history:
Return the simulation telemetry history, sampled every 10 physics steps (up to 5000 frames held). Reply: { total, returned, stride, frames }, where each frame has time, bodies: { name: { pos, vel, angvel, xfrc_applied } }, joints: { name: { pos, vel, qfrc_applied } }, contacts and aeroDiagnostics.

BY DEFAULT YOU GET AT MOST 200 FRAMES spread evenly across the whole history (stride raised to fit; the newest frame is always included). A full buffer is ~14 MB, so narrow it rather than lifting the cap:
- since_time: only frames at or after this sim time (s).
- last: only the newest N recorded frames.
- stride: keep every kth frame (counted back from the newest).
- max_frames: cap on frames returned (default 200; 0 = no cap, the whole window).
- bodies: only these body ids in each frame's bodies.
- include: which sections to return, any of ['bodies','joints','contacts','aero'] (default all).

Filters apply in that order: since_time, then last, then stride/max_frames. Use physics_get_telemetry for just the latest frame.
tools.physics_get_lattice:
Read a lattice body back: every face, as the corners it is made of, in millimetres in the body's own frame.

Faces come back as coordinates rather than as indices into a vertex list, so a face from this reply can be handed straight to physics_lattice_extrude or physics_lattice_delete_faces. Each face also reports which way it faces ('+z', '-x', ...), which tells an outward face from one drawn from the wrong side.

Also returns the counts, the bounds and size in millimetres, and `watertight`. Call it before every edit that names an existing face: a corner that is 0.05 mm out is not that corner, and the edit will be refused.
tools.physics_get_note_cards: Return the current array of note card overlays. Each card has { id, markdown, minimized, x, y }.
tools.physics_get_object:
Return a single object by ID from the physics scene graph with large mesh arrays stripped.

EVERY MESH GEOM IS CHECKED AND THE RESULT IS IN THE REPLY. Alongside vertCount, faceCount and bbox, a mesh carries `watertight`, and when it is not: `boundaryEdges` (edges used by one triangle instead of two), `nonManifoldEdges`, `degenerateTriangles` and `windingInverted`. A mesh that is not watertight draws perfectly and cannot be printed, cast or machined, so read it before you rely on the shape — this is the same guard physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt have always given you, extended to meshes built by hand or imported.
tools.physics_get_objects: Return all objects in the physics scene graph with large mesh arrays stripped (useful to get SCAD and scripts without massive payload).
tools.physics_get_scene: Return the full scene graph (bodies, joints, geoms, scripts), including raw mesh vertex/face arrays. Can be a very large payload for scad/mesh-heavy scenes. Prefer physics_get_scene_summary unless you actually need the raw arrays.
tools.physics_get_scene_summary:
Return a lightweight scene summary: per-node id/name/pos/quat/euler/joints, and per-geom type/size, or for mesh geoms vertCount/faceCount/bbox instead of the raw vertices/faces arrays. Use this for routine checks (did it compile, roughly what size/shape is it) instead of physics_get_scene.

EVERY MESH GEOM IS CHECKED AND THE RESULT IS IN THE REPLY. Alongside vertCount, faceCount and bbox, a mesh carries `watertight`, and when it is not: `boundaryEdges` (edges used by one triangle instead of two), `nonManifoldEdges`, `degenerateTriangles` and `windingInverted`. A mesh that is not watertight draws perfectly and cannot be printed, cast or machined, so read it before you rely on the shape — this is the same guard physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt have always given you, extended to meshes built by hand or imported.

It also reports `stock`: the bench stock (widthMm, depthMm, thicknessMm), the design's size (designMm) and whether it fits, with a note naming by how much it does not. Set the stock with physics_set_environment. designMm is the whole scene, which is what physics_export_machining cuts. With more than one top-level body, `stock.parts` also gives each one's sizeMm and whether it fits on its own (turned 90° if need be), and `partsNote` names any that do not.

EVERY BODY CARRIES `inertial`: what the solver actually uses, read back from the compiled model. massKg; comMm, the centre of mass in the body's own frame; principalInertiaKgM2, the inertia about the principal axes; principalAxesQuat, those axes in the body frame [w,x,y,z]. `totalMassKg` sums every body. This is the figure after densities, hand-set masses and convex decomposition are all applied, so check it instead of running a drop test to infer the mass.

When the scene holds reference pictures (physics_set_reference_image), `referenceImages` lists them: id, plane, center, size in mm, opacity and overlay.
tools.physics_get_schema: Return this app's reference doc, one section at a time: the whole thing is about 75 KB, too much for one read. Called bare it returns the overview and workflow plus `sections`, every section name with its size in characters; pass section=<name> for one of them (gotchas, nodeFields, geomFields, geomTypes, jointFields, openScadNotes, meshNotes, tips, examples, machining, sculpting, lattice and more), or section='all' for everything at once. Read `gotchas` before building scenes: it lists the known failure modes (silent compile errors, text() font issues, the script api. prefix, contype/conaffinity collision pitfalls, hollow-shape collision and others).
tools.physics_get_screenshot: Capture the current rendered frame of the Physics Sim's 3D viewport as a PNG image, exactly as a user would see it (camera angle, colors, lighting). Use this to visually verify a scene's layout, spacing, or shape instead of only inspecting the scene graph numerically. See physics_set_camera to frame a specific view first, and physics_get_camera to check what's currently framed. The frame is rendered on request, so a paused simulation or an idle viewport still gives the scene as it is now. Pass show_colliders: true to outline, for that one frame, what the physics actually collides — each convex piece a hollow body is broken into in its own colour, plus any collision-only or invisible proxy geoms — so a piece bridging a slot or a stale proxy shows at a glance. The viewport's Colliders button shows the same.
tools.physics_get_sculpt: Return a sculpt body's base (for any other mesh body, the name of the geom the brushes work on), whether it has been edited, and its mesh statistics: vertex and face counts, bounds and size in metres, and watertightness. Cheap. Call it between strokes to see the shape growing rather than pulling the whole scene graph, which carries every vertex.
tools.physics_get_state: Return full Physics Sim state: sceneGraph, isPlaying, isLoaded, gravity, wind, density, lastCompileError (string | null: the most recent MJCF/MuJoCo compile failure message, or null if the last compile succeeded). The sceneGraph has its mesh vertex/face arrays stripped, as physics_get_objects does, so the reply stays small; pass include_meshes: true for the raw arrays (one carved part runs to megabytes).
tools.physics_get_telemetry: Return only the latest single frame of simulation telemetry (contains time, bodies: { name: { pos, vel, angvel, xfrc_applied } }, joints: { name: { pos, vel, qfrc_applied } }, contacts, and aeroDiagnostics). Lightweight alternative to physics_get_history.
tools.physics_import_stl: Import a binary or ASCII STL file into the 3D physics simulation. Parses sub-components to infer array spacing and customizer UI parameters (`importMode='scad_parametric'`), raw OpenSCAD polyhedron (`'scad_raw'`), raw 3D mesh (`'mesh'`), or primitive shape approximation (`'primitive'`). Pass path to import an STL file from disk (a Windows path works from WSL); stlData takes the file inline instead and only suits small files. For a big mesh (a sculpt or a scan, tens of thousands of triangles and up) use importMode='mesh': the OpenSCAD modes turn every triangle into script.
tools.physics_lattice_bevel:
Cut the corners off a face, turning an n-gon into a 2n-gon. `amountMm` is how far back along each edge the cut goes.

Use it to make a round face: smoothing a four-cornered cage gives a rounded square, not a circle. Bevel a square into an octagon and smooth that; extrude the octagon first for a cylinder.
