Bevel again for sixteen corners if the part is big enough to show it. For most round faces physics_lattice_circle is simpler.

Only for a face whose corners belong to no other face, such as a lone plate before it is extruded. Its edges must run along an axis or at 45 degrees, and the cut must be under half of every edge.
tools.physics_lattice_bevel_edges:
Chamfer or round EDGES OF THE SOLID, stitching the faces back on either side. `edges` is a list of edges, each a pair of corners [[x,y,z],[x,y,z]] in millimetres, or three corners and up for a whole face's border, so "chamfer that rim" is one call. `radiusMm` is how far back the cut goes; `mode` is 'chamfer' (default) or 'fillet'; `loop: true` grows a single edge to its whole ring first; `mirror` cuts the reflection too.

Use this for edges of a solid, not physics_lattice_bevel. That one cuts the corners off a single FACE whose corners belong to nothing else. This one pulls BOTH faces back from the edge and stitches the gap.

Chamfer and fillet are the same cut and differ only under smoothing: a chamfer's strip is held sharp so it stays a flat chamfer; a fillet's is left soft so physics_lattice_smooth rounds it to an arc of about the radius you asked for. A fillet with smoothing at 0 looks like a chamfer.

Pass every edge you want cut in ONE call. A bevel has to see its neighbours to get the corner where two of them meet right, and calling it once per edge cuts the second from a shape the first already moved. Each edge needs exactly two faces on it, must run along an axis or at 45 degrees, and the cut must leave room on the edges either side (half of each where both ends are being cut). A radius that will not fit is refused and changes nothing.
tools.physics_lattice_bridge:
Join two faces with a band of quads, opening both. Both faces are named by their corners in millimetres, and both are consumed: they become the openings of what is now a tube.

On faces of two SEPARATE shapes it makes them one: a neck, a handle, a strut. On two faces of the SAME shape it bores a tunnel through it. With physics_lattice_inset first, this is how a hole through a part is made.

The faces must have the same number of corners and share none of them. Two whole opposite walls of a box share edges through the walls between them, so they are refused: inset each of them first and join the smaller faces.

Corners are paired by the rotation that puts them closest overall, so the band has no twist, and the result is wound consistently whether it joined two shapes or tunnelled through one.
tools.physics_lattice_circle:
Place a circle, or any regular polygon, as one face. `centre` is [x,y,z] in millimetres, `diameterMm` the diameter, `axis` the plane it lies in ('x'/'y'/'z', the plane's normal, default 'z'), `sides` 0 for a circle or 3/4/6/8… for a regular polygon, `mirror` to place the reflection too. Returns `corners` in millimetres. Pass those straight to physics_lattice_extrude for a cylinder, or physics_lattice_inset for a rim.

At the 0.1 mm grid a polygon rounded to it is within 0.05 mm of the true arc. With `sides: 0` the corner count is worked out from the radius against that budget, so a 2 mm hole stays light and a 60 mm disc is smooth, capped at 64.

What lands is an ORDINARY FACE. Extrude it, bridge two of them for a taper, dimension it, mirror it. Prefer this to drawing an octagon by hand with physics_lattice_faces or bevelling a square twice.
tools.physics_lattice_delete_faces:
Remove faces from a lattice body, named by their corners in millimetres, in any order (a face found reversed counts as the same face). Corners that no longer take part in any face stop being part of the shape.

Use it to open a solid up before bridging it, or to take off a face that was drawn inside-out (physics_lattice_faces can also re-draw that one the other way round). Reports how many were removed and which could not be found.

DO NOT EMPTY THE CAGE. Delete every face and the body has no vertices left, MuJoCo refuses the whole scene with 'at least 4 vertices required', and the body is dropped — while these tools go on reporting ok, because the cage edit itself succeeded. Clearing the starter box to revolve or draw something else is the usual way to hit it. Add the new geometry FIRST and delete the box afterwards; the body is then never empty for a moment.
tools.physics_lattice_dimension:
Set the size or the position of part of a lattice shape by saying the number, rather than by pushing it there. `corners` is the corners to measure, as [x, y, z] points in millimetres — a face's four, an edge's two, or any handful — exactly as physics_get_lattice reports them.

mode 'size' scales them about their own middle on that axis, so both ends move and the rest of the part stays where it is. mode 'position' moves them, measured at the middle of the selection — which for a face is the plane it lies in, so "put this face at 20" is one call.

This is how a part gets to be 40 mm across because the thing it bolts to is. Arriving at that by extruding 7 mm and then 3 mm more is arithmetic nobody should be doing in their head.

Every corner named must be a corner of this shape: a dimension applied to three of the four you meant does not fail, it quietly pulls the part out of square, so a name that matches nothing is refused. Values land on the grid like any other placement — ask for 6.35 on a 0.1 mm grid and the reply reads back 6.4. `changed: false` means the request meant nothing: a size on an axis the selection is flat along, or a number it is already at.
tools.physics_lattice_extrude:
Push one face of a lattice body out along its own axis, walling in the gap it leaves. A box becomes an L, a plate becomes a boss, in one call.

`face` is the face's corners in millimetres, in any order; take them from physics_get_lattice. distanceMm is rounded to whole grid steps and may be negative to push the face in. axis ('x', 'y' or 'z') overrides the direction; by default a face travels along whichever axis it faces.

The face itself is consumed: what was the outside becomes the new cap, and the reply gives the cap's corners so the next extrusion can be chained straight onto it. mirror extrudes the reflected face by the same amount.

A single quad extruded is still an open shell: the side it was pushed off is a hole. Cap it with physics_lattice_faces, wound the other way, or start from the box physics_create_lattice gives you, which is already closed.
tools.physics_lattice_faces:
Draw faces on a lattice body. `faces` is a list of faces, each a list of THREE OR MORE corners [x, y, z] in MILLIMETRES in the body's own frame. Use quads wherever possible: Catmull-Clark smoothing puts a dimple at every triangle corner — but an outline that is genuinely a polygon should be sent as one face rather than cut into quads, because a profile split into pieces extrudes into pieces with walls between them. A T is eight corners; an L is six.

Corners do not have to exist yet; a corner that lands where one already is reuses it, which joins the new face to the shape. Points are snapped to the 0.1 mm grid and `snappedBy` reports the largest correction made. A snap of half a step is rounding; a snap of five is a mistake in the numbers.

WINDING DECIDES WHICH WAY A FACE POINTS: corners counter-clockwise seen from outside the solid. A face wound the other way is invisible in the viewport and a hole in the exported file. Check the `normal` physics_get_lattice reports rather than assuming.

mirror ('x', 'y' or 'z') also adds each face's reflection through the body origin, with the winding reversed. Returns what was added, what was skipped and why, and the cage's new counts.
tools.physics_lattice_inset:
Shrink a face inside itself by `amountMm`, leaving a ring of quads around it. `face` is the face's corners in millimetres, in any order; the reply gives the corners of the new smaller face.

This is the start of every hole. Inset each wall first, then physics_lattice_bridge the two smaller faces to bore a tunnel. Inset and then delete the middle for a hole in a plate. Inset and then extrude for a raised panel or a recess.

Only a face lying flat on to an axis can be inset. The inset must also be less than half the face's width.
tools.physics_lattice_orient:
Turn every face of a lattice body to agree with its neighbours and point outwards, and report how many were turned.

A face's winding decides which side of it is solid. A face wound inwards draws wherever backfaces are shown and is lost wherever they are culled, so a part can look finished and export full of holes. Faces drawn by hand take their winding from the order their corners were given.

Every reply from a lattice tool carries `inconsistent`, the number of faces that are inward or at odds with their neighbours. When it is not zero, call this. It is safe to call when it is zero; it does nothing and says so.

Run it before physics_lattice_wall: a wall is offset along the surface's own normals, so on a shape whose normals disagree it is thickened in both directions at once.
tools.physics_lattice_revolve:
Sweep a profile about one of the body's axes, the way a lathe does. `profile` is two or more points [x,y,z] in millimetres in the order they run along the profile, `axis` is the spindle ('x'/'y'/'z', default 'z'), `degrees` is how far round (1 to 360, default 360), `closed: true` joins the last profile point back to the first (a solid ring rather than a shell), `throughMm` moves the axis line off the origin, `segments` overrides how many stops it takes.

Use it for anything turned: a boss, a spigot, a knob, a funnel, a wheel rim. physics_lattice_extrude makes prisms only.

The profile does not have to be drawn first: corners that are not there yet are created, so a whole turned part is one call. HOW FAR EACH POINT SITS FROM THE AXIS IS ITS RADIUS; there is no second number. A point sitting ON the axis becomes the pole, so a cone is a two-point profile: [[0,0,40],[30,0,0]] about 'z' is a 60 mm cone 40 mm tall. Less than 360 leaves both ends open.
tools.physics_lattice_sharpen:
Mark edges of a lattice body sharp, so smoothing rounds everything except them. Pass sharp:false to let them round off again.

Catmull-Clark rounds every edge it is given. Crease the edges that should stay crisp: the rim of a housing, the flat faces of a bracket, the top edge of a knob.

`edges` is a list of edges, each exactly two corners [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]] in millimetres. Take them from the `corners` physics_get_lattice reports; creases already set come back per face as `sharpEdges`. Only an edge some face runs along can be creased; a diagonal across a quad is not an edge.

A corner where three or more sharp edges meet is held in place entirely, so the corner of a box stays square while its faces round. mirror also marks the reflected edge.

loop:true grows each edge into the whole ring it belongs to: the rim of a shell, the top of a cylinder, the seam around a boss. Prefer it to listing a ring edge by edge. A loop runs on through four-way corners and stops where there is no straight on, so on a plain box (every corner three-way) it is just the edge given.

An entry of THREE OR MORE corners is read as a face, and marks that face's whole border. Use that for the rim of a cap: the corners around one are three-way, so no loop runs through them.
tools.physics_lattice_smooth:
Set how many Catmull-Clark passes a lattice body's mesh is built with: 0 (the cage itself, flat faces and hard edges), 1, or 2.

Use this to get curves from a grid: a coarse cage of a few dozen quads, smoothed, rather than a finer grid with thousands of corners.

The CAGE is unchanged and stays what you edit; what changes is the mesh built from it, which is what the physics, the STL and every CAM path see. Quads smooth cleanly and triangles do not, so a shape that will be smoothed should be built out of quads.
tools.physics_lattice_wall:
Give a lattice body a wall thickness in millimetres, turning the surface into a closed shell. Pass 0 to take it off again.

A lattice is a SURFACE. A slicer, a mold and a CAM job all need a closed solid, so a shape that reports watertight:false needs a wall or a cap before export.

The offset runs INWARDS, so a shape drawn as the outside of a part keeps the dimensions it was drawn with. The wall is built after smoothing, so it follows the rounded surface rather than the cage, and the rim where the two surfaces meet is held sharp.

The cage is untouched and goes on reporting itself as open; the mesh built from it is closed. A SHAPE THAT IS ALREADY CLOSED IGNORES THIS, and the box physics_create_lattice hands you is closed. So hollowing that box out means deleting a face first — the one the part opens on, usually the bottom — and then walling the open surface that leaves. Wall a closed box and nothing at all happens.
tools.physics_list_presets: Return available physics scene preset names.
tools.physics_load_preset: Load a physics scene preset. Preset names come from the app's PRESETS registry. Call physics_list_presets for the current list rather than relying on a hardcoded set. Also accepts 'user:<name>' to load a preset the user saved in the app.
tools.physics_machine_arm:
Deliberately CANNOT arm the machine. It exists to give a clear answer rather than leave you guessing why motion is refused.

Arming is a click in the app, by the person standing next to the machine: ARM. That is the one thing in this tool set an agent may not do for itself. If you need to move the machine and it is not armed, ask the user to click it — do not retry, and do not look for another route.

The permission lasts about an hour and covers jogging, zeroing, probing, framing and carving. They can end it at any moment with DISARM in the same banner, which also cancels whatever is running.
tools.physics_machine_cancel: Stop the job and drop the rest of the program. Never gated. The line it reached is kept, so it can still be picked up with physics_machine_resume_from_line. Soft-resets the controller, which leaves it in alarm if it was moving — unlock and re-home before cutting again.
tools.physics_machine_connect:
Open the link to the machine. `transport` is 'usb' or 'wifi'; WiFi also needs `deviceId`.

USB opens a native port-picker that only the person at the keyboard can answer, so it only works if they are sitting there. WiFi has no such prompt and is the transport to prefer — and on a carve it is the better one anyway: through a Tekno Box the device runs the program itself, so a four-hour job survives the laptop being shut.
tools.physics_machine_disarm: Give the permission back before it lapses, and stop anything running. Needs no arming itself. Worth calling when a carve has finished and nothing further is planned.
tools.physics_machine_disconnect: Close the machine link. Does not stop a job — cancel or e-stop first if one is running.
tools.physics_machine_estop:
Emergency stop: soft-reset the controller and stop the spindle, at once. Never gated and never refused.

Reach for this the moment something looks wrong — a cut in the wrong place, a sound that is not right, the user saying stop. Position is lost and the machine needs re-homing and re-zeroing, which is a small price. Do not deliberate about it.
tools.physics_machine_frame_job:
Trace the outline of the stock with nothing cutting. Needs the machine armed.

On a laser the guide beam is lit for this — `guidePower` sets how bright — so the operator can watch exactly where the outline falls on the material. That is the whole point: it answers 'is the stock where the job thinks it is, and is it big enough' in seconds, before anything cuts.

Do this after zeroing and before physics_carve_scene.
tools.physics_machine_goto_origin: Lift to a safe height, then travel to the work origin. `safeZMm` default 5. Needs the machine armed.
tools.physics_machine_home:
Run the homing cycle ($H) against the limit switches. Needs the machine armed. Only works where homing is enabled ($22=1).

Homing establishes machine coordinates; it does not set the work origin and does not make a stale Z datum trustworthy.
tools.physics_machine_jog:
Move the tool by a relative distance: x, y and z in mm, optional feedRate (default 1000). Positive Z is up. At least one axis required. Needs the machine armed.

A GRBL `$J=` jog, so it leaves modal state alone and can be cancelled mid-move. The reply carries the position after the move, read back from the controller rather than assumed.
tools.physics_machine_list_devices: List the Tekno Boxes paired to this account, with whether each is online. Pass one of these ids as physics_machine_connect's deviceId to cut over WiFi. Read-only.
tools.physics_machine_pause:
Feed hold: decelerate and stop without losing position or discarding the planner. Never gated.

The spindle is deliberately left running and the tool is left in the cut — a stationary bit in contact with the work is what burns wood and welds itself into acrylic. Resume with physics_machine_resume.
tools.physics_machine_preview_resume:
What a resume from a given line would do, without doing it. Read-only, never gated.

Returns the preamble it would send and whether the reconstructed state is uncertain. The depth in that preamble is the number worth checking against the workpiece in front of the operator before committing. A program that was streaming when the browser went away is restored from a checkpoint on the next load, so this and resume_from_line now work across a reload, a sleep or a power cut — not only within the session that started the job.
tools.physics_machine_probe_surface:
Probe a grid across the stock and return the heights, for levelling a carve against a bed or workpiece that is not flat. Optional `cols`/`rows` (default 3x3) and `bounds`. Needs the machine armed.

A 0.2mm dish across a 300mm bed is enough to cut through a 0.4mm veneer at one end and not scratch it at the other.
tools.physics_machine_resume: Pick a paused job back up. Needs the machine armed. A tool-change or material pause parks the machine, so resuming drives it back to the cut first; a feed hold only needs releasing.
tools.physics_machine_resume_from_line:
Restart a job that ended badly, part way through. Needs the machine armed. `fromLine` is the program line to pick up at.

This is the tool that turns a dead three-hour carve into twenty lost minutes. Line eleven thousand of a program means nothing on its own — the units, coordinate system, feedrate, spindle speed and depth were all established thousands of lines earlier — so the program is replayed WITHOUT being sent to work out that state, and a short preamble puts the machine back into it: retract, spindle up to speed, move over the point it stopped at, then descend at a feedrate rather than a rapid.

Call physics_machine_preview_resume first and read out the depth it names. And note what this does NOT check: a resume after a snapped cutter is a resume onto a different tool, whose length makes the existing Z datum wrong in the direction of driving into the work. Re-zero Z first.

A job interrupted by the tab closing, the laptop sleeping or the power going off is also resumable: the program and the line it reached are checkpointed to this browser's storage as it streams (and to the account on PhysBox Pro, which is the only option for a program too big for localStorage). The app offers it back on load and on tab focus. That kind of resume is flagged `restored`, and it is the dangerous one: the controller has been through a power cycle, so it is not homed, its tool is unknown, and the work must still be clamped exactly where it was. Home, confirm the work origin and re-zero Z before resuming one.
tools.physics_machine_settings:
The controller's `$$` settings — max rates, accelerations, steps/mm, homing configuration — as read when the link opened. Read-only.

An empty result with a `note` means the controller never answered `$$`, which is NOT the same as a controller with no settings: the figures are unknown, so do not reason about travel limits or feed ceilings from their absence. This app's run-time estimates depend on these, and says when it is falling back to an assumed profile.
tools.physics_machine_status:
Report the machine: whether it is connected, its GRBL state, work and machine coordinates, live feed and spindle, the trim percentages, and how far through a job it is. Read-only and never gated.

`armed` is the field that decides what else you can do. False means every command that moves an axis will be refused until the person at the machine allows it; `armedUntil` is when that permission lapses on its own. Call this before anything else here.
tools.physics_machine_trim:
Trim a running job without stopping it: `feed` and `spindle` take a step of 10, 1, -1 or -10 (percent) or 'reset'; `rapid` takes 100, 50 or 25. Never gated.

What to reach for when a carve is chattering or a cut is scorching, where the alternative is aborting onto material that has been cut into and can no longer be registered.

STEPS, NOT TARGETS: GRBL has no command to set a figure, so 87 is rejected rather than silently ignored. Nudge and check with physics_machine_status.
tools.physics_machine_unlock:
Clear GRBL's alarm lockout ($X). Needs the machine armed.

Routine after a boot lockout. NOT routine after a limit trip or a reset mid-motion: the machine has lost its position and unlocking does not give it back. Home it before cutting.
tools.physics_machine_zero_all: Set X, Y and Z all at once where the tool is standing. Needs the machine armed. The quick setup when the tool is already parked at the corner of the stock at cutting height.
tools.physics_machine_zero_xy: Set the current XY position as the work origin. Needs the machine armed. Jog the tool over the corner of the stock first. Written with `G10 L20`, a real work offset that survives a reset.
tools.physics_machine_zero_z:
Set work Z0. Needs the machine armed. Two ways:
- `touchPlateMm` (default 12): probes down onto a conductive plate of that thickness and puts Z0 the plate's thickness below the contact point. Pass the real figure — a wrong one is a wrong datum, silently.
- `here: true`: records where the tool is standing right now as Z0, with an optional `offsetMm`. This is what to use when the operator has wound the tool down onto the stock by eye, which on a carve is common and perfectly legitimate.

Either way this is what clears the app's `needsZZero` flag. The flag is set the moment a connection opens and again at every tool change, because GRBL keeps the Z offset in EEPROM across sessions, tools and stock — a datum that reads back as valid may belong to a different setup entirely, and nothing in a status report says whether this operator has zeroed this Z since.
tools.physics_measure:
Measure a distance between two points, or the angle at a corner between three. `start` and `end` are points [x,y,z] in METRES in the world frame (the same frame physics_get_objects reports); `corner` turns it into an angle measured at that point; `withinMm` is how far it may snap (default 3); `snap: false` measures exactly the points given.

Each end snaps to the nearest feature: a box's analytic corners, a cylinder's axis and end centres, a mesh vertex, or THE CENTRE OF ANY CIRCLE the neighbouring vertices lie on. That last one makes hole-centre-to-hole-centre measurable on a boolean result, where the document no longer holds the cylinder that cut the hole.

It measures the DRAWN scene, not the document: transforms applied, booleans evaluated, lattice cages smoothed, walled and recentred. Every reply says what each end landed on and how far it had to move (`movedByMm`). If `movedByMm` is large, you aimed at the wrong thing. Distances come back in millimetres and metres, with the per-axis parts in `deltaMm`.

ORIENTATION: pass `body` (id or name) instead of start/end to ask which way a body points — "how far is the phone leaning". `axis` picks one of the body's own axes, 'x', 'y' or 'z' (default z). Returns fromVerticalDeg (angle between that axis and world up), fromHorizontalDeg, headingDeg (direction of its horizontal part, from +X towards +Y, null when vertical), axisWorld and quat. Read from the simulation's latest frame when it has run (source 'simulation', atTime), else from the body as authored (source 'authored'). physics_run_headless reports every body's final tilt in `final` without a separate call.
tools.physics_paint: Brush colour onto PART of a geom's surface, as dabs at points on it. Use it for markings: the pips of a die, a stripe down a roller, eyes on a head. Paint adds no geoms, no collisions and no mass. at is [x,y,z] or a list of them, in the GEOM'S OWN frame in metres (the same frame as the geom's pos/size, so a box of size [0.01,0.01,0.01] has its +Z face at z=0.01 and its corners at x,y=±0.01), and every point in one call is one stroke: the five pips of a die face are a single call. radius is the brush radius in metres (default 0.008). rgba is [r,g,b], each 0..1. flow is how much coverage one dab lays down, 0..1 (default 1, full strength; lower values tint, and dabs that overlap build up). Pass erase:true to take paint off instead. Paintable geom types are box, sphere, ellipsoid, cylinder, capsule and mesh; a mesh is painted on the vertices it already has, so a coarse mesh holds only coarse marks. Painted geoms are re-tessellated finely, which is visual only. Errors if no vertex falls within radius of any point; that means the point is not on the surface, usually because it was given in world space instead of the geom's frame.
tools.physics_apply_pattern:
Lay a surface pattern or TEXT — lettering in any Google font, wood grain, flutes, fish scales, kumiko, cracked earth and the rest of the Generators patterns — on ONE FACE of a part that already exists, the way the T key does in the app. The pattern is drawn and exported (STL, 3MF, relief carve, solid machining, slicing, the laser's engrave layer) but the PHYSICS SEES THE PLAIN SHAPE: it is surface detail, not geometry the simulation pays for.

`at` is a point on the face in the BODY's own frame in millimetres, as for physics_cut; `normal` is the way the face looks (optional — without it the nearest surface in any direction is taken). The face is grown from that point out to the part's sharp edges and covered whole: a box's whole top, a cylinder's whole side, a dish and over a rounded rim. A part with no edges at all (a sphere, a capsule, a sculpted blob) cannot be covered whole without tearing the pattern, so there it covers the side within 75° of the point and the reply says `capped: true`. `stopAtDeg` sets that limit on any face (180 is none); it is rarely needed. Calling it on a face that already has a pattern EDITS that pattern: only what you pass changes. `remove: true` takes it off. `preview: true` builds it and reports, without changing the scene — use it to see what face and size a point picks.

`pattern` is a pattern id; a wrong one is refused with the full list and each pattern's options. `options` are that pattern's own settings (sizes in mm, e.g. fluted {pitchMm, profile}, scales {scaleMm}). `depthMm` (default 1.5) is how deep it is engraved, or with `emboss: true` how far it stands proud. `borderMm` (default 2) leaves a plain rim round the face. `cellMm` (default 0.4) is the detail: smaller is crisper, slower and heavier. `twistDeg` turns it on the face; `scale` multiplies every feature's size. `color` ([r, g, b] each 0..1, or '#rrggbb') paints the part the pattern moves in a colour of its own: the letters of text, engraved or embossed, or the sunk ground of an engraving / the raised ground of an embossing; the untouched face keeps the body's colour. It is drawn in the viewport and written to the 3MF as paint, so a multi-filament slicer gets it as a second filament. 'none' takes it off; on an edit, leaving it out keeps it. The reply gives it back as hex. Every pattern also takes the layout options: layoutAlign ('fit' stretches the pitch to whole repeats edge to edge, 'centre', 'free'; on regular repeats only), frameMm with frameStyle ('plain', 'groove', 'raised', 'sunk') and frameGrooveMm, symmetry ('none', 'mirror_x', 'mirror_y', 'quarter', 'k3'..'k12' kaleidoscope), fadeMm and softenMm. Patterns include ornament (lotus_mandala, thai_tiles, rosette), board-fitted layouts (raised_panel, tiles, contour_rings, spiral), parquet/herringbone, weave, tartan, water_drop, ocean, landscape, cobblestone, honeycomb, greek_key, truchet and star_lattice.

TEXT: `pattern: 'text'` puts lettering on the face, in any Google font (shift+T in the app). Options: text (newlines for more lines), fontFamily (a Google Fonts family name, e.g. 'Roboto', 'Cinzel', 'Pacifico'; default Roboto), fontWeight ('300','400','500','700','900'; the nearest the family has), heightMm (capital-letter height, default 8), letterSpacingMm, lineSpacing (baseline to baseline in letter heights, default 1.6), align ('left','centre','right'). path is the line it runs along: 'straight' (default); 'arc' round a circle of arcRadiusMm centred on the face, arcSide 'top' (over the top, reading clockwise) or 'bottom' (under it, reading left to right, sharing the same ring -- one of each makes a seal); 'wave' with waveAmpMm and waveLengthMm; 'custom' along pathD, an SVG path in mm, y down as SVG draws it, placed by pathAlign ('start','centre','end'). pathOffsetMm slides it along its path. offsetXMm/offsetYMm move it from the middle of the face; boxMm draws a rectangle line round straight text, boxPadMm from it. On a cylinder the text is placed once, centred on `at`, not repeated round. Engrave (default) cuts the letters in; `emboss: true` raises them; depthMm is the depth or height. cellMm defaults to 0.25 for text. The font is fetched when the call is made; an unknown family is refused (ok:false). The reply's options leave out the saved letter outlines.

`projection` is how a curved face is laid flat for the pattern: 'auto' (default) projects a flat face, unrolls a cylinder's side, and unwraps anything else so the pattern's cells stay square; 'planar', 'cylindrical' and 'unwrap' force one. A pattern taken all the way round a cylinder is resized slightly so it meets itself (`wrap.scaled` in the reply); one that does not repeat is blended across the join (`wrap.blended`). A tube that is not a cylinder is cut open on the far side from `at`, and the cut is left plain (`seam`).

The reply gives the face's size (`faceMm`), its area, the projection used, how much the layout stretches the pattern (`stretchPercent` — above 15 means it visibly distorts), the depth actually used (less than asked on a tight curve) and any warnings. ok:false with the reason when it cannot go on: the face is already patterned by an overlapping pattern, or the depth would fold the surface through itself.

IMAGE / HEIGHT MAP: pattern 'image' raises a picture from the face (emboss) or cuts it in (engrave), light parts high. Give the picture as image_path (a PNG or JPEG on disk, read by the MCP server), or options.image as a data URL or an http(s) URL. It is decoded once into a grey grid of at most 1024 px a side and the file is not kept. Options: mapping 'white-high' (default) or 'white-low'; fit 'stretch' (default: over the whole face), 'contain' (keep its shape, centred) or 'width' (widthMm wide), with offsetXMm/offsetYMm for the last two; blurPx 0-8 smooths pixel steps. Round a cylinder's whole side (pick the side with stopAtDeg 180) it goes once round, stretched to the circumference, the middle of the picture on the point picked: draw a height map as the cylinder's unrolled side, its left and right edges matching, and it closes on itself with no seam. cellMm defaults to 0.25; fine detail on a big face is limited by the triangle budget, and a warning says when the detail was coarsened.
tools.physics_knife:
Divide a part with a flat plane, the way the K key (Knife) does in the app: leave a SEAM on its faces, or with `cut: true` cut it right through into separate bodies.

`at` is a point the plane passes through and `normal` the direction square to it, both in the BODY's own frame (`at` in millimetres), as for physics_cut and physics_apply_pattern. By default the plane leaves a seam: the part stays one solid with the same physics, but every face the plane crosses (as far as that face's sharp edges) becomes two faces, and a pattern laid with physics_apply_pattern stops at the seam as it stops at a sharp edge. That is how to put two different patterns on one face, or a pattern on half of one: halve a sphere through its middle, then pattern each half. Seams are listed per geom as `faceSplits` in physics_get_object. The reply lists the geoms divided and how many faces each. `remove: true` takes off the seam passing nearest `at` (within 5 mm; `normal` is not needed).

`cut: true` cuts right through: every separate piece becomes its own body in place, keeping the part's colour, with its mass shared out by volume and exact convex colliders. The first piece keeps the part's id. Each piece keeps the patterns and seams of the faces it was cut from: a pattern the cut ran through is laid afresh on both pieces, each over its own part of the face. The reply lists the pieces with their ids, volumes and how many patterns and seams each kept. ok:false when the plane does not cut right through the part, or for a seam when it divides no face (it misses the part, or runs along an edge).
tools.physics_probe_sculpt:
Find where the surface is. Pass `at`: [x, y, z] or a list of them in the body's own frame, and get back, for each, the nearest point ON the surface, the outward normal there, and how far off the guess was. Nothing is changed.

Use it to get coordinates to sculpt and paint with. The bounding box from physics_get_sculpt locates only the extremities; the belly of a bird, the side of a head, the inside of a hand have to be probed for. Probe a handful of guesses in one call, then sculpt with the points it returns. physics_paint errors if no vertex falls within its radius, so probe before painting too.
tools.physics_reset: Reset the physics simulation to its initial state.
tools.physics_run_headless:
Run the physics simulation headlessly for N ticks. Returns trajectory: [{time, bodies:{name:{pos,vel,angvel,xfrc_applied}}, joints:{name:{pos,vel,qfrc_applied}}, contacts:[{geom1,geom2,dist}], aeroDiagnostics:{name:{relSpeed,alpha,CL,CD,force,torque}}}], warnings:[string]. Does not affect the live view. Use this to verify scene behaviour programmatically (a projectile lands in the right place, a pendulum reaches the right angle, a body comes to rest at the expected position) before calling physics_play for visual presentation. PAYLOAD CONTROL: pass stride=N to keep only every Nth trajectory frame (plus the final frame) and bodies=[names] to include only those bodies per frame. A full per-tick all-body trajectory is ~500KB per 900 ticks and long runs can blow the response window without decimation. For most verification (final position, trajectory shape, lap progress) stride=10 loses nothing that matters.

EVERY REPLY SAYS WHETHER IT FINISHED. `ticksRequested` is what you asked for, `ticksSimulated` is what actually ran, and `truncated` says whether the run stopped early; when it did, `truncationReason` is 'diverged', 'nan' or 'frame-cap' and `truncationDetail` explains it in words.

'diverged' is the one to expect. MuJoCo does not throw when a model goes unstable — it silently resets the state and the clock back to zero and keeps stepping. A run over a scene that blows up therefore used to come back as a full-length trajectory that was really several restarted runs stitched together, with times that climbed, jumped back and climbed again. Now the first tick that fails to advance the clock ends the run and says so. If you see it, the scene is unstable: look for very light bodies, stiff contacts, huge scripted forces, or a composite with too many segments.

Kept frames are exactly `stride` ticks apart, always in ascending time order, with the final tick appended.

The reply also carries `final`: whether the run ended at rest and how each body ended. final.settled is true only when every body moved under 1 mm/s and turned under 0.5 °/s throughout the last half second, and no body was rocking (its tilt reversing twice in the last second by more than 0.2°); it is false for a run shorter than half a second. final.bodies[id] gives posMm, tiltDeg (its own +Z against world up), turnedDeg (since the first frame), speedMmS, angSpeedDegS, settled and rocking. Read it instead of scanning the trajectory: the first still-looking frame of something rocking is one end of a swing.
tools.physics_save_preset: Save the current active physics scene graph and note cards as a custom user preset, the way the Save button does: in this browser and, when signed in, in the account too; a scene too big for the browser goes to the account alone. Waits for the account and returns `savedTo` ('browser', 'account' or 'browser and account'), `message`, and a `warning` when signed in but the account did not take it. A failure returns `error` with what to do about it.
tools.physics_sculpt:
Brush the surface of a sculpt body or of any other mesh body: an imported STL, a mesh loaded from a scene file, a compiled OpenSCAD part. On a body with several meshes it brushes the first one that is not the output of a boolean. A primitive and a boolean body are refused. A stroke on a big imported mesh (500k triangles) takes about half a second; pass dynamicTopology false on a mesh that is already dense enough. `at` is [x, y, z] or a list of them in the BODY'S OWN frame in metres (the same convention as physics_paint). Each point is one dab, and the whole call lands as a single stroke and a single undo step. Points do not need to be exactly on the surface: each is snapped to the nearest point on it, and the normal there sets the brush direction.

A point further from the surface than one brush radius is reported in `missed` rather than applied, and each miss carries `nearest`, the point that would have worked. Feed that back in. This matters on the animal and figure bases, where a coordinate guessed from the bounding box is often off the surface.

brush is one of: draw (push out along the normal; the general-purpose one), inflate (swell the whole area, for mass rather than a feature), smooth (average out lumps and brush marks), flatten (pull the area onto a plane, for a facet or a flat face), pinch (draw the surface together for a ridge, a crease or a sharp edge), grab (take hold and drag; the brush for gross shape, and the only one that needs `delta`, without which it does nothing).

invert reverses the brush: draw carves in, inflate deflates, pinch spreads. symmetry mirrors every dab across a plane through the body's origin: pass 'y' for anything with a left and a right. THE FIGURE BASES ALL FACE +X, so their left and right lie along Y. Mirroring 'x' on a head reflects front to back. The default is 'x'. radius is in metres (default a sixth of the body's longest side), strength is 0..1 (default 0.5). dynamicTopology (default true) lets the brush add triangles as it goes, so detail is not limited by the base's resolution; turn it off once the shape is settled and you are only smoothing. detail is the target edge length as a fraction of the radius (default 0.25); smaller is finer and much more expensive.

AN EXACT DEPTH: depthMm (draw only) is the most one stroke raises or carves, measured from the surface where the stroke began. Keep dabbing and the surface stops there, a flat floor at that depth, so 'draw' with invert and depthMm 2.5 carves a 2.5 mm groove in one call instead of a bowl that deepens with every pass. A second stroke goes on from the new floor. hardness 0..1 (default 0) is the share of the radius that works at full strength before the edge falls away: 0 is a soft blend, 0.8 a flat-ended punch with a steep wall, for crisp eye sockets and slits. For a feature under about 2 mm, use a radius about half its width with hardness 0.7 or more.

Returns the new vertex/face counts, whether the mesh is still watertight, how many dabs landed, and the misses. Check the count is growing as you expect: a stroke that reports applied:0 changed nothing at all.

`maxDisplacement` is how far the furthest vertex travelled, in metres, and it is NULL whenever `topologyChanged` is true — which is most strokes, because dynamicTopology is on by default and a brush that adds triangles renumbers the mesh, leaving nothing honest to measure against. Null means not measured, not nothing happened; read `applied`, `moved` and the vertex count for that.
tools.physics_sculpt_cut:
Cut a sculpt body, or any other mesh body physics_sculpt can brush, with scissors: a polygon swept straight through the whole body, taken out. A polygon in the middle of the body makes a hole through it; one that runs over the edge cuts that piece off. The body stays a sculpt, so you can go on brushing it, including the new cut faces. Prefer this to physics_cut on a sculpt: physics_cut turns it into a boolean, which ends sculpting.

`polygon` is three or more [x, y, z] points in the BODY'S OWN frame in metres, the same convention as physics_sculpt. It is projected onto a plane and swept along `direction` (default: the polygon's own normal) far enough to go right through the body both ways, so only its outline matters, not its depth. For example, a square of side 0.04 in the XY plane with direction [0, 0, 1] drills a square hole straight down through the top of a base.

mode 'remove' (the default) takes the swept prism out; 'keep' keeps only what lies inside it and takes everything else away. cap (default true) closes the cut with new flat faces so the body stays a solid; cap false leaves the hole open, so the sculpt becomes a shell you can see into. An open shell will not print or machine, and reports watertight false.

A CUT THAT SPLITS THE CLAY MAKES ONE BODY PER PIECE. The largest piece stays on this body; each of the others becomes a new sculpt body at the same pose, listed in `bodies` (this body first), so any of them can be moved, brushed or removed with physics_delete_object on its own. A split cannot be taken back with physics_undo_sculpt (its history for the body is cleared); the editor's undo reverses it.

Returns facesBefore/facesAfter, `pieces`, `bodies` when it split, the usual sculpt summary (of this body) and undoDepth. A cut that does not split the clay is undone with physics_undo_sculpt, which shares its history with physics_sculpt. A cut that would remove all of the clay, or a polygon that encloses nothing, is refused with an error and changes nothing.
tools.physics_set_camera: Point the 3D viewport camera at an explicit pose: position and optional target, both MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z]. Or pass preset to reset to a built-in view (this also clears any prior explicit pose): 'perspective' (the diagonal 3/4 pose, not aligned to any world axis), or one of the orthographic drawing views — 'topDown' (looking down -Z, +Y up the screen), 'front' (looking along +Y from the -Y side, +Z up) and 'side' (the right-hand view, looking along -X, +Y to the right, +Z up). The drawing views are framed on the scene's content; an explicit position always goes back to perspective. dims=true|false switches the Dims overlay, alone or with a preset: in a drawing view it marks the selected body (or every body when none is selected) in mm — true sizes along each body's own axes (overall width and height, a chain between the face edges, hole centres and the steps of round parts, ⌀ on rounds seen side on), the diameter of every hole, sphere or rod seen end-on with equal holes counted ('2× ⌀8'), the angle of a turned part, and each body's origin from its parent's. physics_get_camera returns what it drew as `dimensions`. Use this rather than rotating a body to line a face up with a fixed camera.
tools.physics_set_color: Set a body's base colour. rgba is [r,g,b] or [r,g,b,a], each 0..1; alpha below 1 renders translucent. Omit geomName to colour every geom of the body, which is usually what you want after physics_import_stl: an imported mesh often arrives as several geoms. Colour is decorative only: it never reaches the physics, the MJCF or any exporter. For markings on part of a surface (pips, stripes, a logo, eyes on a face) use physics_paint instead of adding decorative geoms.
tools.physics_set_environment: Update physics environment. gravityZ is negative for downward gravity (e.g. -9.81). windX/windY add lateral fluid drag. density is the density of the surrounding fluid in kg/m3 and it adds DRAG, not buoyancy: MuJoCo's fluid model here pushes back against motion and lifts nothing. A balloon in a scene with density 1.2 still falls. To float something, apply the weight of the fluid it displaces yourself, from that body's script: `api.applyForce([0, 0, rho * volume * 9.81])`. See schema.buoyancy. floorFriction controls ground grip. floorBounce: 0=no bounce (default), 1=maximum bounce. Sets floor dampingRatio to (1-floorBounce), averaged with each contacting geom's own dampingRatio. fidelity is 'standard' (default) or 'print': print makes contact as stiff as the 1 ms timestep allows (resting penetration about 0.04 mm instead of millimetres) and brings Split for Print's exact pin and socket colliders to life, so dowels and pegs really go into their holes; use it for millimetre parts that have to fit together. It is saved with the scene and undoable. All fields optional. STOCK: stock_width_mm, stock_depth_mm and stock_thickness_mm set the board on the bench — the stock every carve and export uses and the design is checked against (the same numbers as the status bar). Describe the user's real board here rather than modelling it into the design; the reply and physics_get_scene_summary's `stock` then say whether the design fits it (designMm, fits, and a note such as 'The design is 5 mm wider than your stock.').
tools.physics_set_note_cards:
Replace the note card overlays. Pass noteCards: [{ id, markdown, minimized, x, y }]. One card is the norm; id can be any unique string, minimized false, and x/y in the 20-40 range put it clear of the toolbar. Call this after every physics_build_scene or physics_update_scene, and again whenever an edit changes what the card claims. Pass an empty array to clear all cards.

The markdown should read like a museum label for THIS scene, in this shape:
- `# Title` naming the actual thing built ("Ball Bearing Race"), not its category.
- A sentence or two on what it is and what it does when you press Play.
- `## Dimensions`: the sizes that matter, in millimetres and kg, as a short list or table: overall extent of the assembly, the size and mass of each significant body, and any gap, radius, or spacing a reader would want the number for. Read them off the geoms you just wrote (geom `size` is a HALF-extent for box and ellipsoid, so a size of [0.1, 0.1, 0.1] is a 200 mm cube) rather than restating the prompt.
- `## Physics`: the mechanism: which joints, what constrains what, the equation or effect being demonstrated, and any figure worth quoting (period, gear ratio, equilibrium speed).
- `## Try it`: two or three specific things to change, naming the actual body or field to change and what will happen.

Write the numbers you built with; do not round them into vagueness ("about a metre wide") and do not describe the plumbing ("built via MCP", "MuJoCo convex hull"). The built-in presets' cards are the house style: physics_load_preset one and physics_get_note_cards to read it.
tools.physics_set_sculpt_base: Swap a sculpt body's base shape. DESTRUCTIVE: the mesh is replaced outright and any sculpting done on it is gone, so ask the user before calling it on a body they have worked on. Use it to start again, or to correct a base chosen wrongly at the outset. The new base comes out at the size the body already is.
tools.physics_resize_sculpt: Scale a sculpt body so its longest side is sizeMm millimetres (1 to 2000), or give sizeMm as [width, depth, height] to size each axis on its own (null keeps one as it is): [null, null, 58] squashes a ball into a pumpkin, the panel's Clay mm X/Y/Z. Everything scales together, sculpting included, about the body's origin, so a base sitting on z = 0 still does. Not destructive. Use it when the clay came out the wrong size; it is better to give physics_create_sculpt the right sizeMm at the start, since a brush radius chosen for one size is wrong for another. It clears physics_undo_sculpt's history for the body (its entries are at the old scale); the editor's undo reverses the resize.
tools.physics_sculpt_carve:
Carve the clay with a cutter dragged along a path: the panel's Carve tool (key 8). The cutter is swept along `path` (points in the body's own frame, metres, each snapped onto the surface; give enough points to follow a curve, as the stretch between two is straight) and subtracted, so the groove has the cutter's own clean walls and rim, exactly widthMm across and depthMm deep along the surface normal, whatever the clay's triangles are. Use it for anything that must be crisp or exact: a mouth, an eye socket, a rib valley, a lettered line. Brushes (physics_sculpt) are for soft form.

profile 'round' (default: a ball-nosed U), 'v' (a crease) or 'flat' (square walls, flat floor). fill: true treats the path as a closed outline and cuts out the whole area inside it to the depth, with a rounded edge: the cutter's centre runs on the outline, so the pocket reaches widthMm/2 beyond it. symmetry mirrors the path. taper (0 to 0.5) narrows and shallows the cutter to a point over that share of the path at each end: a rib valley that fades into the stem. angleDeg leans the cutter to one side of the path, for a slanted cut or an undercut.

mode 'add' joins clay on instead: a round tube widthMm across swept along the path, which may leave the surface. Start just inside the clay and run out into the air for a stem, a horn or a handle; with taper it thins to its tip. depthMm is not used.

Runs in a worker. Replies like physics_sculpt_cut: facesBefore/facesAfter, pieces, bodies when it split, and the sculpt summary. Undo with physics_undo_sculpt.
tools.physics_toggle_play: Toggle play/pause of the physics simulation.
tools.physics_undo_lattice:
Take the last lattice operation back off. The last 8 made through these tools are kept per body, newest first, and every reply carries `undoDepth` so you know how far back you can go.

Separate from the editor's own undo, so it never swallows a person's work. Use it for an extrusion that went the wrong way rather than building over it: an extrusion in the wrong direction leaves side walls inside the solid.
tools.physics_undo_sculpt:
Take the last stroke or cut back off. Use it for a stroke that landed wrong rather than correcting it with more strokes.

The last 8 strokes and cuts made through physics_sculpt and physics_sculpt_cut are kept, per body, newest first; every stroke's reply carries `undoDepth` so you know how far back you can go. This is separate from the editor's own undo, so it never swallows a person's work.
tools.physics_update_object: Update a single object by ID in the physics scene graph. The updates parameter is a partial object containing any fields from nodeFields (such as scad, pos, euler, script, joints, or geoms) to update and recompile on-the-fly.
tools.physics_update_scene: Replace the full scene graph. sceneGraph is a bare array of SceneNode objects (same convention as physics_build_scene's bodies param). Full control but requires complete valid structure. Waits for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for MJCF to settle before responding. The response is { ok, error?, nodeCount }, so check `ok`/`error` directly rather than polling physics_get_state. Can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies. After the scene lands, write its note card with physics_set_note_cards; nothing else does. The default card says "Interactive 3D rigid-body physics scene". Replace it as part of building the scene.
tools.physics_load_scene_file: Load a Mesh scene from a JSON file on this machine — the format Export JSON writes ({nodes, noteCards, copilotMessages}) — into the connected Mesh tab, replacing the current scene. The MCP server reads the file itself, so a scene of many megabytes (sculpted or carved meshes run to 10-20 MB) never passes through a tool call; prefer this to physics_update_scene for any scene you already have on disk. `path` is a path on the machine the MCP server runs on (absolute or ~-relative), in that OS's own form. Loads like the app's Import JSON: the whole graph as written (no default-filling), its note cards and chat, the sim stopped, and no preset selected, so Save will not overwrite one. Waits for the model to compile and returns {ok, error?, nodeCount, noteCardCount, file, megabytes}. Size limit: none from the session that owns the hub; about 32 MB when called from a secondary MCP session, whose commands are relayed through the hub (the tool refuses up front rather than lose the connection).
tools.physics_validate_scad:
Validate OpenSCAD code and return whether it compiles successfully. On success also returns vertCount, faceCount, and boundingBoxM (the compiled mesh's bounding box in meters) so you can sanity-check real-world size before loading it into a scene. If the compiled bounding box is implausibly large (diagonal >20m), the response includes a `warning` field flagging that you likely forgot to wrap the design in scale([0.001,0.001,0.001]). OpenSCAD designs are typically authored in millimeters, but MuJoCo units are meters, so an un-scaled millimeter design compiles ~1000x too large. On failure returns an error message.

COMPILES ARE FAST. The geometry engine is Manifold, so a plate with twenty-seven holes at $fn=32, or an M8 thread through 20 mm, evaluates in a fifth of a second; $fn=180 on a few dozen features is still a second or two. Nothing is rejected for being dense, and this call waits two minutes for it. Leave $fn at what the machines here can show — 32 is finer than anything they can cut.
tools.use_session: Send every later command for an app to one particular browser tab. port is the app's port (5175 for Mesh) and session_id comes from list_sessions. Selecting a tab that has gone away is refused, and the error lists the ids that do exist.

choosingTheRightTool.ruleOfThumb: Build detailed scenes in ONE call to physics_build_scene (or add parts with physics_add_object) using declarative body features instead of making 20 sequential tool calls or hand-writing raw triangle arrays.
choosingTheRightTool.mechanicalPartsWithHolesThreadsRounding: Use primitive geoms + declarative `cuts: [...]`, `roundEdges: [...]`, `patterns: [...]`, and `paint: [...]` directly on the body descriptor in physics_build_scene / physics_add_object / physics_update_object, OR boolean geoms (`csg: 'difference' | 'intersection'`).
choosingTheRightTool.extruded2DProfilesWithHoles: Use `type: 'extrude'` (or `'prism'`) with `polygon: [[x,y], ...]` (metres), optional `holes: [[[x,y], ...]]`, and `height` (metres) on a geom or body.
choosingTheRightTool.turnedOrAxisymmetricParts: Use `type: 'lathe'` (or `'revolve'`) with `profile: [[r,z], ...]` (metres) on a geom or body, OR a declarative lattice `{ lattice: { empty: true, subdiv: 1, ops: [{ op: 'revolve', profile: [[xMm,0,zMm], ...] }] } }`.
choosingTheRightTool.conesWedgesToriTubes: Use parametric geom types directly: `cone` (`size: [r, hh]`), `pyramid` (`size: [hx, hy, hh]`), `wedge` (`size: [hx, hy, hz]`), `torus` (`size: [R, r]`), `tube` / `pipe` (`size: [outerR, innerR, hh]`).
choosingTheRightTool.subdivisionAndGridPolyhedra: Use declarative `lattice: { sizeMm: 40, subdiv: 1, thicknessMm: 0, ops: [{ op: 'extrude' | 'inset' | 'bevel' | 'bevel_edges' | 'circle' | 'revolve' | 'bridge' | 'faces' | 'delete_faces' | 'sharpen' | 'dimension' | 'orient' | 'smooth' | 'wall', ... }] }` on the body, or pass `ops: [...]` to `physics_create_lattice`.
choosingTheRightTool.organicClayShapes: Use declarative `sculpt: { base: 'sphere' | 'head' | ..., strokes: [...], cuts: [...] }` on the body, or pass batch `strokes: [...]` to `physics_sculpt`.
choosingTheRightTool.curvedTracksAndRamps: Set `isCurve: true` and `curvePoints: [[x,y,z], ...]` (Z-up metres) on the body.
choosingTheRightTool.customPolyhedra: If you must supply raw triangles (`type: 'mesh'`), pass `verticesZUp: [x0,y0,z0, ...]` in standard MuJoCo Z-up metres (auto-converted to Y-up `vertices` and `renderVertices`, with inside-out closed meshes auto-flipped). Avoid hand-typing hundreds of coordinates when `extrude`, `lathe`, `lattice`, or `scad` can express the shape in 5 lines.

geomSizes.box: half-extents [hx, hy, hz]. Full dimensions are 2*hx × 2*hy × 2*hz
geomSizes.capsule: [radius, half-height]: a cylinder of half-height hh capped with hemispheres of radius r. Or use fromto to specify endpoints directly. ALWAYS supply both elements (or fromto): a 1-element [radius] does not error, it silently falls back to half-height = radius and collapses the geom into a tiny stub pill at its pos.
geomSizes.ellipsoid: semi-axes [rx, ry, rz]: a sphere stretched independently on each axis
geomSizes.plane: ignored. MuJoCo treats it as an infinite ground plane
geomSizes.cone: [radius, halfHeight] (or `radius` and `height` fields in metres) — closed outward-wound cone mesh
geomSizes.pyramid: [hx, hy, halfHeight] (or `width`, `depth`, `height` in metres) — 4-sided pyramid mesh
geomSizes.wedge: [hx, hy, hz] (or `width`, `depth`, `height` in metres) — right-triangular prism / ramp mesh
geomSizes.torus: [majorRadius, tubeRadius] (or `majorRadius`, `tubeRadius` in metres) — watertight torus ring in XY plane around Z axis
geomSizes.tube: [outerRadius, innerRadius, halfHeight] (or `outerRadius`, `innerRadius`, `height` in metres; alias `pipe` / `hollow_cylinder`) — hollow cylinder / pipe mesh
geomSizes.extrude: 2D polygon prism (alias `prism`): provide `polygon: [[x,y], ...]` in metres, optional `holes: [[[x,y], ...]]`, and `height` in metres (or `size: [halfHeight]`). Centered on Z by default (`centered: false` spans z=0..height).
geomSizes.lathe: revolved 2D profile around Z axis (alias `revolve`): provide `profile: [[r,z], ...]` in metres and optional `segments` (default 24).
geomSizes.mesh: arbitrary triangle mesh via `verticesZUp` (preferred, Z-up metres) or `vertices` (Three.js Y-up metres) + `faces`. Defaults to `dynamic: true` so body `pos`/`euler`/`quat` and geom `pos`/`euler`/`quat` always position the mesh in Z-up space.

jointTypes.free: 6-DOF unconstrained; body falls freely under gravity. Use for dropped objects.
jointTypes.hinge: 1-DOF rotation around axis. Specify axis:[x,y,z]. Use for wheels, doors, pendulums. For a bearing, lid or arm that should hold its angle, set frictionloss (dry friction, N*m); damping alone only slows it.
jointTypes.slide: 1-DOF translation along axis. Specify axis:[x,y,z]. Use for pistons, rails. For a slide that should hold its place, set frictionloss (dry friction, N).
jointTypes.ball: 3-DOF rotation (ball-and-socket). Use with stiffness+damping for springs, sway, or frictionloss for a joint that holds its pose.

geomFields.name: string: unique identifier (required)
geomFields.type: GeomType (required — includes parametric mesh shorthands cone, pyramid, wedge, torus, tube, extrude, lathe)
geomFields.pos: [x,y,z]: local offset from body origin in MuJoCo Z-up space. Works on all geoms including dynamic meshes.
geomFields.euler: [roll,pitch,yaw] degrees: local rotation, alternative to quat
geomFields.fromto: [x1,y1,z1, x2,y2,z2]: capsule/cylinder endpoints in local space, overrides size/pos/quat
geomFields.mass: number: override density-based mass for this geom
geomFields.density: number kg/m3: what the geom is made of. MuJoCo weighs a geom by its volume at a default density of 1000 (water), so a hollow or airy shape left at the default comes out absurdly heavy. Ignored when mass is set. Prefer it over mass for anything that may be rescaled, since it keeps weighing the right thing. Oak ~700, pine ~500, concrete ~2400, steel ~7800, acrylic ~1190, PLA ~1240; a tree crown, a hedge or any other mostly-air volume is single digits. DENSITY IS PER GEOM, so one body can mix materials: an acrylic ring with steel bolts is a ring geom at 1190 plus cylinder geoms at 7800 on the same body. A SCAD body compiles to ONE mesh geom with one density, so for a mixed part keep the SCAD for the main material and add the others as extra primitive geoms on that body (a bolt that should not collide can take contype 0 / conaffinity 0), or split the part into bodies welded together. physics_get_scene_summary's inertial.massKg shows the result.
geomFields.friction: [slide, spin, roll]: contact friction coefficients. slide: tangential sliding (0=icy, 2=rubbery). spin: torsional around contact normal (typical 0.005). roll: rolling resistance (typical 0.0001).
geomFields.contype: integer bitmask: collision group this geom belongs to
geomFields.conaffinity: integer bitmask: which groups this geom collides with
geomFields.solref: [timeconst_s, dampingRatio]: contact spring parameters. timeconst_s: spring time constant in seconds, must be >= 5x timestep (0.005s minimum). Lower = stiffer contact. dampingRatio: 1.0 = critically damped (no bounce), 0.0 = underdamped (max bounce), ~0.2 = lively bouncing. Contact between two geoms averages both dampingRatios: set floor to 0.0 and ball to 0.2 to get 0.1 effective ratio. Default (no solref set): [0.02, 1.0] = stiff, no bounce.
geomFields.solimp: [d0, d1, width, midpoint, power]: contact impedance. d0: min impedance (0.8-0.99), d1: max impedance (0.99-0.9999), width: transition width, midpoint: where transition is centered, power: curve shape. Higher d0/d1 = harder contact, less penetration. Typical bouncy: [0.99, 0.9999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2].
geomFields.verticesZUp: number[]: PREFERRED for custom meshes: flat [x0,y0,z0, ...] in standard MuJoCo Z-up metres. Automatically populates Three.js Y-up `vertices` and `renderVertices`, and auto-flips closed meshes if wound inside-out.
geomFields.vertices: number[]: mesh only: flat [x0,y0,z0,...] in Three.js Y-up space (X=right, Y=up, Z=toward camera). Optional if `verticesZUp` or `renderVertices` is supplied.
geomFields.faces: number[]: mesh only: flat triangle indices [i0,j0,k0,...] with outward-facing (CCW) winding. Closed meshes with uniformly negative signed volume are automatically flipped right-side out.
geomFields.polygon: number[][]: for `type: 'extrude'`: 2D `[x, y]` vertices in metres
geomFields.holes: number[][][]: for `type: 'extrude'`: optional array of 2D `[x, y]` hole loops in metres
geomFields.profile: number[][]: for `type: 'lathe'`: 2D `[r, z]` profile points in metres revolved around Z
geomFields.dynamic: boolean: defaults to `true` on all `type: 'mesh'` geoms so body `pos`/`euler`/`quat` and local `geom.pos`/`euler`/`quat` always position the mesh in Z-up space.
geomFields.renderVertices: number[]: dynamic mesh only: flat [x0,y0,z0,...] in raw MuJoCo Z-up space. Auto-derived from `verticesZUp` or `vertices` if omitted.
geomFields.margin: number: expand contact surface outward by this amount (meters). Useful to prevent sinking.
geomFields.gap: number: dead zone inside margin where no contact force is applied.
geomFields.paint: {res, idx, rgba}: brushed vertex colour laid down by physics_paint or declarative `paint` on the body.
geomFields.dentYieldNs: number — newton-seconds above which this MESH surface takes a permanent crater. Cosmetic: contact keeps using the undented shape. Transient.
geomFields.dentDepthPerNs: number — metres of depth per newton-second over the yield.
geomFields.dentMaxDepth: number — hard cap on how deep one spot can be pushed, in metres.
geomFields.pierceImpulseNs: number — N*s past which the surface is holed clean through instead of dented. Keep it well above dentYieldNs. Cosmetic: contact keeps using the whole surface.
geomFields.deformCollision: boolean — make damage to this surface real to the contact solver rather than only visible. Costs a model rebuild AND a convex decomposition per blow; off by default.

nodeFields.name: string: display name and MuJoCo XML name
nodeFields.type: always 'body' (or shorthand geom type when `geoms` is omitted)
nodeFields.pos: [x,y,z]: position relative to parent (or world for root)
nodeFields.euler: [roll,pitch,yaw] degrees: body orientation, alternative to quat
nodeFields.static: boolean: if true (or `fixed: true` / `dynamic: false`), omits the default free joint so a top-level body is fixed in world space
nodeFields.geoms: SceneGeom[]: one or more geoms defining shape (optional if body-level `type`/`size` shorthand, `lattice`, `sculpt`, `isCurve`, or `scad` is used)
nodeFields.cuts: DeclarativeCut[]: array of hole/slot/dish/hardware cut specs `{ shape?: 'cylinder'|'slot'|'dish'|'counterbore'|'nut_trap'|'insert'|'insert_boss'|'bearing', at?: [xMm,yMm,zMm], normal?: [nx,ny,nz], diameterMm?, widthMm?, lengthMm?, depthMm?, threadPitchMm?, size?: 'M3'|'M4'|..., bore?, fitMm? }` applied automatically when the body is built or updated
nodeFields.roundEdges: DeclarativeRound[] | DeclarativeRound: `{ edges?: 'all'|'top'|'bottom'|'vertical'|'inside'|number[], sizeMm: number, mode?: 'round'|'bevel' }` (or array of them; alias `roundings`) applied automatically after cuts
nodeFields.patterns: DeclarativePattern[]: array of surface textures `{ at: [xMm,yMm,zMm], normal?: [nx,ny,nz], pattern: string, depthMm?: number, emboss?: boolean, options?: {...} }` applied automatically to the body faces
nodeFields.paint: DeclarativePaint[]: array of paint strokes `{ at: [x,y,z] | [[x,y,z],...], rgba: [r,g,b,a?], radius?: number, flow?: number, geomName?: string }` (in metres) applied automatically after CSG
nodeFields.lattice: { sizeMm?: number, empty?: boolean, subdiv?: 0|1|2, thicknessMm?: number, ops?: LatticeOp[] }: builds a lattice body inline in a single pass. Each op in `ops` is `{ op: 'extrude'|'inset'|'bevel'|'bevel_edges'|'circle'|'revolve'|'bridge'|'faces'|'delete_faces'|'sharpen'|'dimension'|'orient'|'smooth'|'wall', ... }` in mm.
nodeFields.sculpt: { base?: 'sphere'|'cube'|'cylinder'|'humanoid'|'quadruped'|'bird'|'fish'|'hand'|'head', sizeMm?: number, strokes?: SculptStroke[], cuts?: SculptCut[] }: builds a sculpted clay body inline in a single pass. sizeMm is the longest side, applied before the strokes; without it the base is 240 mm across and a stroke with no radius uses 0.04. Strokes take depthMm and hardness as physics_sculpt does.
nodeFields.joints: SceneJoint[]: joints to parent (empty = fixed to world)
nodeFields.coupleTargetId: id of body to gear-couple first joints with
nodeFields.weldTargetId: id of body to rigidly weld (closed-loop constraint)
nodeFields.connectTargetId: id of body for ball-socket point constraint
nodeFields.script: JavaScript control script running at 1000 Hz. IMPORTANT: all functions must be called with the 'api.' prefix, e.g. api.getTime(), api.setVelocity([...], 'bodyName'). Bare calls like getTime() will throw ReferenceError. Available: api.isKeyPressed(keyName), api.getPosition(bodyName), api.getVelocity(bodyName), api.getAngularVelocity(bodyName), api.getOrientation(bodyName), api.setPosition(pos, bodyName), api.setVelocity(vel, bodyName), api.setAngularVelocity(angvel, bodyName), api.getMass(bodyName), api.getJointPosition(jointName), api.getJointVelocity(jointName), api.applyForce(forceVec, bodyName), api.applyTorque(torqueVec, bodyName), api.applyJointForce(jointName, forceVal), api.setActuatorControl(actuatorName, ctrlVal), api.getTime(), api.getWind(), api.log(msg). Local variables reset every step: keep anything that must last between steps (an integral, a timer, a phase) on api.state, a per-body object that survives edits made mid-play and is cleared by Reset. Mutate it (api.state.n = (api.state.n || 0) + 1); assigning api.state itself is ignored. Keep it to plain values, arrays and objects — no functions. To launch a body with an initial velocity on the first tick: 'if (api.getTime() === 0) { api.setVelocity([vx, vy, vz], "bodyName"); api.setAngularVelocity([wx, wy, wz], "bodyName"); }'
nodeFields.scad: string: raw OpenSCAD source code to procedurally compile into a dynamic mesh geometry. In physics_update_object, null or "" removes the source and keeps the last compiled mesh (or the geoms sent in the same call) as a plain mesh.
nodeFields.isComposite: boolean: if true, this body is emitted as a MuJoCo <composite> (a chain of auto-generated, auto-jointed segments forming a smooth curve/cable/rope) instead of using this node's own geoms/joints/children directly. Use this instead of chaining many capsule geoms with fromto to approximate a curve. See compositeType/compositeCount/compositeSize/compositeCurve.
nodeFields.compositeType: 'cable'|'grid'|'rope'|'cloth': shape of the composite. 'rope' is remapped to MuJoCo's 'cable' composite type internally; for a smooth 1D curve (rope, cable, mustache, tentacle, vine) use 'cable' or 'rope'. Default 'cable'.
nodeFields.compositeCount: string (NOT an array): space-separated segment counts, e.g. "25 1 1" for a 25-segment 1D cable. More segments = smoother curve but more DOF. Default "15 1 1".
nodeFields.compositeSize: string (NOT a number): total extent of the composite before curving, e.g. "1.5" for a 1.5m cable. Default "1.5". The segments take MuJoCo's DEFAULT DENSITY of 1000 kg/m3, and nothing here overrides it, so the radius is the only thing setting the mass: a 0.9 m cable at radius 0.003 weighs about 26 g, which is four times a helium balloon and will simply hold it down. For anything meant to read as string or thread, radius 0.0004 or so.
nodeFields.compositeCurve: string: MuJoCo composite curve-shape spec (space-separated per-axis codes+params), e.g. "s 0 0" for straight, or a cosine/other MuJoCo composite curve code for a pre-curled shape. Not validated client-side; a malformed string only surfaces as a MuJoCo XML compile error. The chain is laid out along the BODY'S +X before any curve is applied, so a cable meant to hang or stand needs the body turned: euler [0, -90, 0] points it up +Z.
nodeFields.compositePrefix: string: name prefix for the auto-generated segment bodies (default `${name}_`). The last segment's auto-generated name is `${compositePrefix}B_last`, needed if you want to weldLastToId it to something.
nodeFields.weldLastToId: string: id of another body to rigidly weld the composite's LAST segment to (e.g. anchoring both ends of a rope/cable). Only used when isComposite is true. Compare to the general weldTargetId, which welds this node's own body, not a composite's generated last segment.
nodeFields.isCurve: boolean: RIGID curved track. A Catmull-Rom spline through curvePoints is decomposed into many small convex box geoms, so collision follows the real (even concave) curve and balls roll along it. Omit geoms and joints: geoms are auto-generated and the body defaults to static (welded to world). Contrast with isComposite, which makes a floppy rope/cable.
nodeFields.curvePoints: number[][]: body-local Z-up control points, e.g. [[-1.6,0,1.4],[-0.55,0,0.45],[0.45,0,0.12],[1.6,0,0.7]]. The spline IS the rolling surface (segment boxes sit half a thickness below it).
nodeFields.curveSegments: number: how many box segments approximate the spline (default 28; more = smoother)
nodeFields.curveClosed: boolean: wrap the spline into a seamless closed loop (oval/circuit tracks). Default false.
nodeFields.curveBank: number: bank (roll) angle in degrees about the travel direction; positive raises the left-of-travel edge. For a counter-clockwise loop use a NEGATIVE bank to raise the outside edge (the oval_track preset uses -18).
nodeFields.isSculpt: boolean: a free-form sculpted body. Its mesh is not derived from parameters; the sculpt tools own it. Set by physics_create_sculpt or declarative `sculpt` on the body.
nodeFields.sculptBase: string: which base shape it was started from. See schema.sculpting.bases.
nodeFields.sculptVersion: number: bumped whenever the mesh is replaced wholesale, so the viewport reloads it. Managed for you.
nodeFields.sculptEdited: boolean: whether any stroke has been applied since the base was set.
nodeFields.weldBreakForceN: number — newtons of pull this weld survives before it shears off. Omit and it never breaks. Transient: reset puts it back.
nodeFields.weldBreakTorqueNm: number — newton-metres of twist this weld survives. Either limit alone is enough.
nodeFields.weldBreakHoldSteps: number — consecutive overloaded steps required (default 3), guarding against contact-onset solver spikes.
nodeFields.shatterImpulseNs: number — newton-seconds of impulse that breaks this body into pieces. Omit and it never shatters. Transient: reset makes it whole.
nodeFields.shatterPattern: 'uniform' | 'radial' — radial crowds the small pieces around the point of impact (default).
nodeFields.shatterSpread: number — extra outward speed per piece, m/s.
nodeFields.shatterSeed: number — fixes which pieces, so a scene breaks the same way twice.
nodeFields.shatterDepth: number — how many times the PIECES may break again when they land (0 default, 2 max). Later generations split into at most four chips that do not collide with each other, and the world holds at most 60 shards.

jointFields.name: string: unique joint name
jointFields.pos: [x,y,z]: joint anchor point in local body space
jointFields.damping: number: velocity-proportional resistance (for free joints, scales drag force/torque to decay velocity and spin uniformly)
jointFields.stiffness: number: spring constant pulling back to springref
jointFields.frictionloss: number: dry joint friction — the torque (N*m, hinge) or force (N, slide) the joint holds against before it moves, and resists with while it moves. Use it for anything that should stay where it is left: a lid propped open, a lamp arm, a stiff print-in-place hinge. damping cannot do this: it fades to nothing as the joint slows, so a damped lid still falls shut, only later. To hold against gravity it must exceed the load, e.g. a 0.2 kg lid with its centre 50 mm from the hinge needs > 0.2*9.81*0.05 = 0.1 N*m. Ball joints apply it to all three axes; free joints ignore it.
jointFields.limited: boolean: whether range limits are active
jointFields.range: [min,max]: joint limits in degrees (hinge) or meters (slide)
jointFields.crumpleTorqueNm: number — N*m past which this joint stops being rigid and folds, permanently. Omit and it behaves as always.
jointFields.crumpleRangeDeg: [number, number] — how far it may fold once it has given, in degrees.
jointFields.crumpleDampingAfter: number — damping written into the joint the moment it gives, so it settles into its new shape rather than swinging into it.

contactPhysicsTips.howContactParamsAreBlended: When two geoms touch, MuJoCo averages their solref and solimp values. This means the floor's dampingRatio directly dilutes a ball's bounce: ball dampingRatio 0.2 + floor dampingRatio 0.0 = effective 0.1 (bouncy). Ball 0.2 + floor 1.0 = effective 0.6 (dead). The built-in floor uses dampingRatio=0.0 so it does not kill bounce.
contactPhysicsTips.defaultContactParams: Geoms with no solref/solimp use the scene default: solref=[0.02, 1.0] (stiff, no bounce), solimp=[0.99, 0.9999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2]. Only set solref/solimp on geoms where you want non-default behaviour.
contactPhysicsTips.makingBouncyObjects: Set solref=[0.04, 0.2] and solimp=[0.99, 0.9999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2] on the geom. dampingRatio 0.2 gives lively but controlled bounce. The UI Bounciness slider (under Physical Material in the properties panel) sets dampingRatio directly, keeping timeconst at 0.04s.
contactPhysicsTips.stabilityLimit: solref[0] (timeconst) must be at least 5x the simulation timestep (0.001s), so minimum 0.005s. Lower values make the contact spring too stiff for the integrator and cause energy explosion. 0.04s is a safe, stiff-feeling default.
contactPhysicsTips.frictionComponents: friction=[slide, spin, roll]. slide (0-2): tangential friction, 0=icy, 1=normal, 2=rubbery. spin (0-0.05): torsional friction around contact normal. roll (0-0.01): rolling resistance; keeps spheres from rolling forever.

meshNotes.staticMesh: No dynamic field (or dynamic:false). Still collides normally (convex hull, like any mesh geom) and, on a body with no joint, never moves. If the body DOES have a joint, a static-flagged mesh geom simulates and collides correctly while its on-screen render stays frozen at its initial baked position, since it never re-reads xpos/xmat. Reserve dynamic:false for mesh geoms on bodies that never move; a jointed body's mesh geoms default to dynamic:true unless you say otherwise. Vertices in Three.js Y-up WORLD space: the render ignores the body's pos and quat entirely, so a mesh authored in body-local coordinates draws at the world origin instead of where the body is (its collision and any primitive geoms on the same body are still at the body's pos, so the two visibly disagree). Either bake the body's position into the vertices or set dynamic:true. Good for scenery, decorative structures, visual shells around primitive collision proxies.
meshNotes.dynamicMesh: dynamic:true (or omitted on a jointed body, where it's defaulted). Render re-syncs from the body's xpos/xmat every frame, so the mesh visually tracks a joint or a drag. Collision (convex hull) happens the same way as a static mesh; dynamic doesn't change that. Vertices in Three.js Y-up for collision, renderVertices in raw MuJoCo Z-up for rendering (auto-derived from vertices if you don't supply it).
meshNotes.renderVerticesRule: renderVertices = Y-up vertices with Y↔Z swapped: (x,y,z)→(x,-z,y). No centroid subtraction. MuJoCo recenters the mesh internally; xpos tracks the body frame correctly.
meshNotes.faceWinding:
Use outward-facing CCW winding: each triangle's (v1-v0)x(v2-v0) must point AWAY from the interior. Wrong winding causes inside-out contact normals and objects sinking through surfaces.

IT ALSO HAS A VISUAL SYMPTOM THAT DOES NOT LOOK LIKE A WINDING BUG. Geoms are drawn single-sided, so a backwards triangle is not drawn at all. A whole surface built backwards therefore reads as a body that is HALF TRANSPARENT — you see through its near face to the inside of its far wall — which sends you looking at rgba alpha and materials instead of at the geometry. If a body looks see-through, call physics_get_scene_summary and read `windingInverted` before anything else. The California relief preset shipped inside out and was read as a transparency bug until someone summed its signed volume.
meshNotes.bodyPos: For a dynamic mesh whose Y-up base is at Y=0, set body_pos=[0,0,0]. The mesh will render with its MuJoCo origin at ground level. Adjust body_pos.z to raise/lower.
goodUseCases: Dynamic convex polyhedra (pyramids, crystals, custom shapes)
meshNotes.closedSurfaces:
A MESH YOU BUILD BY HAND IS NOT CLOSED UNLESS YOU CLOSED IT, and nothing in the viewport will tell you. The renderer draws triangles; it does not care whether they enclose a volume. An export does: a slicer, a mold, a casting pattern and a CAM job all need a solid, and all of them refuse or quietly mangle a surface with holes in it.

The usual way to get this wrong is to assemble a shape out of PIECES — a chain of tubes along a path, a stack of rings, a row of slabs — and emit each piece as its own open-ended shell. Consecutive pieces line up so the seams are hidden inside opaque geometry and the model looks perfect from every angle, while every joint is a pair of open rims. Cap every piece, or skin the whole run in one pass sharing a ring between neighbours.

Three faults are fatal downstream: an open edge (used by one triangle instead of two), inside-out winding, and a zero-area triangle from two coincident vertices.
